questions.chapterName: Chapter 1: Core Elements of Professionalism
questions.stem: The ABIM Physician Charter is built on three fundamental principles. Which of the following is NOT one of those principles?

choices.text: Primacy of patient welfare
Patient autonomy
Social justice
Physician accountability

questions.explanation: The three fundamental principles of the ABIM Physician Charter are: (1) Primacy of patient welfare, (2) Patient autonomy, and (3) Social justice. Physician accountability is one of the ten professional responsibilities, not a fundamental principle.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 1: Core Elements of Professionalism
questions.stem: The ABIM Physician Charter distinguishes between three fundamental principles and ten professional responsibilities. Which of the following is a professional responsibility rather than a fundamental principle?

choices.text: Just distribution of resources
Primacy of patient welfare
Patient autonomy
Social justice

questions.explanation: Commitment to just distribution of finite resources is one of the ten professional responsibilities in the ABIM Physician Charter. Primacy of patient welfare, patient autonomy, and social justice are the three fundamental principles upon which the responsibilities are built.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 1: Core Elements of Professionalism
questions.stem: Which professional responsibility is most closely associated with a commitment to lifelong learning?

choices.text: Improving quality of care
Professional competence
Professional responsibilities
Scientific knowledge

questions.explanation: Commitment to professional competence requires physicians to maintain medical knowledge and clinical skills throughout their careers. This includes staying current with advances in their field such as AI.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 1: Core Elements of Professionalism
questions.stem: A radiologist receives a lucrative consulting arrangement from a medical device company. According to the ABIM Physician Charter, the most relevant professional responsibility is:

choices.text: Managing conflicts of interest
Patient confidentiality
Honest communication with patients
Social justice

questions.explanation: Managing conflicts of interest is an explicit professional responsibility in the ABIM Physician Charter. Physicians must recognize, disclose, and manage conflicts of interest that arise from financial or personal relationships.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 1: Core Elements of Professionalism
questions.stem: The principle of 'social justice' in the ABIM Physician Charter most closely refers to:

choices.text: Involvement of physicians in local and national politics
Dedication to serving the interest of the patient
Fair distribution of health care resources
Empowering patients to make informed decisions about their treatment

questions.explanation: Social justice as a fundamental principle of the ABIM Physician Charter refers to fair distribution of health care resources. Physicians should work toward equity in access to health care.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 1: Core Elements of Professionalism
questions.stem: A radiologist consults one of his subspecialty colleagues to assist in the interpretation of a challenging study. Which of the following radiology-specific ethical considerations does this situation fall under?

choices.text: Misleading billing arrangements
Agreements for provision of high-quality care
Self-referral
Professional limitations

questions.explanation: Radiologists should be aware of their limitations and to seek consultations in clinical situations where appropriate. Any limitations should be appropriately disclosed to patients and referring physicians.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 1: Core Elements of Professionalism
questions.stem: Which of the following is most accurate regarding the concept of 'patient autonomy' as a fundamental principle of medical professionalism?

choices.text: Patients should be empowered to make informed decisions about their own care
Patients should be able to decide the most appropriate imaging modality for a given clinical indication
Physicians must be dedicated to serving the interest of the patient
Physicians should never exploit patients for sexual advantage or personal financial gain

questions.explanation: Patient autonomy means that patients should be empowered to make informed decisions about their own medical care. Patients' decisions about their care must be paramount, as long as they are in keeping with ethical practice and do not lead to demands for inappropriate care.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 1: Core Elements of Professionalism
questions.stem: Which of the following LEAST describes the commitment to professional responsibilities?

choices.text: Being respectful of one another
Remediation and discipline of members who fail to meet professional standards
Promptly communicating medical errors to patients
Defining and organizing the educational and standard-setting process for current and future members

questions.explanation: Answer choice C describes the commitment to honesty with patients, not the commitment to professional responsibilities. All other answer choices are elements of the commitment to professional responsibilities.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 1: Core Elements of Professionalism
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the responsibility of physicians to ensure the appropriate use of new medical information?

choices.text: Commitment to honesty with patients
Commitment to scientific knowledge
Commitment to improving the quality of care
Commitment to professional competence

questions.explanation: Commitment to scientific knowledge is an ABIM professional responsibility requiring physicians to uphold scientific standards, promote research, and apply scientific knowledge to practice.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 1: Core Elements of Professionalism
questions.stem: The principle of 'primacy of patient welfare' in the ABIM Physician Charter is based on:

choices.text: Market forces which dictate which therapies and procedures a patient is eligible for
Societal pressures which require physicians to be subservient to patients
Centrality of trust between patients and physicians
Administrative bylaws outlined by the Board of Trustees at any given healthcare institution

questions.explanation: The ABIM Physician Charter states that trust is central to the physician-patient relationship, which must not be compromised by market forces, societal pressures, or administrative exigencies.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 1: Core Elements of Professionalism
questions.stem: In the context of radiology ethics, what is the purpose of the report signature?

choices.text: To identify the attending physician who is overseeing the work of a resident
To identify the physician under whose name the procedure will be billed
To absolve other interpreters of liability in the event of a lawsuit
To signify that the person signing the report has personally reviewed the images and agrees with the content of the report

questions.explanation: Radiologists should not sign a report or claim attribution of an imaging study interpretation that was rendered by another physician, making the reader of a report believe that the signing radiologist was the interpreter.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 1: Core Elements of Professionalism
questions.stem: Which of the following best exemplifies the ABIM principle of 'commitment to improving quality of care'?

choices.text: Identifying common causes of medical errors and implementing initiatives to reduce such errors
Working with multiple radiology stakeholders to increase throughput of MRI and CT scanners at the hospital
Creating a tiered payment system such that patients with lower income pay less for imaging studies
Promoting research and creation of new scientific knowledge

questions.explanation: Physicians should work collaboratively with other professionals to continuously improve the quality of healthcare, including reducing medical errors, increasing patient safety, improving utilization of healthcare resources, and optimizing outcomes of care.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 1: Core Elements of Professionalism
questions.stem: According to the ABIM Physician Charter, which of the following describes a commitment to a just distribution of finite resources?

choices.text: Making full-body MRI scans more accessible to lower-income populations
Selecting the most expensive equipment to provide premium quality
Avoiding superfluous tests and procedures
Referring patients to physicians within the same health system exclusively

questions.explanation: Commitment to just distribution of finite resources includes the scrupulous avoidance of superfluous tests and procedures to reduce patient exposure to harm, decrease health expenses, and improve access to resources for patients who need them.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 1: Core Elements of Professionalism
questions.stem: Self-regulation within the medical profession refers to:

choices.text: Individual physicians managing their own work schedules
Physicians collectively maintaining ethical and professional standards
Hospital credentialing committees determining physician privileges
State medical boards independently licensing physicians

questions.explanation: Commitment to maintaining trust by managing conflicts of interest and self-regulation means the profession collectively maintains and enforces ethical and professional standards, including addressing misconduct within the profession.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 1: Core Elements of Professionalism
questions.stem: A radiology group is considering implementing an imaging ordering system that benefits a company in which several partners have financial stakes. The most ethical course of action is to:

choices.text: Proceed if the system provides adequate clinical functionality
Have non-conflicted staff decide without disclosing the conflict to others
Refer the decision to hospital administration without disclosing the conflict
Disclose financial interests and recuse conflicted parties from the decision

questions.explanation: The ABIM Physician Charter's commitment to managing conflicts of interest requires physicians to disclose financial relationships and recuse themselves from decision-making when conflicts exist.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 1: Core Elements of Professionalism
questions.stem: Which of the following most accurately describes 'medical professionalism' as articulated in modern frameworks like the ABIM Physician Charter?

choices.text: Wearing appropriate attire and maintaining decorum in the workplace
A set of values, behaviors, and relationships that underpins public trust in physicians
The technical mastery of one's medical specialty
Adherence to hospital policies and avoiding malpractice

questions.explanation: Medical professionalism encompasses a set of values, behaviors, and relationships that underpin public trust in physicians. It goes beyond technical competence to include ethics, integrity, and accountability.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 1: Core Elements of Professionalism
questions.stem: The ACR Code of Ethics specifically addresses which of the following issues unique to radiology?

choices.text: Misleading billing arrangements
Surgical technique standards for radiologists performing procedures
Physician payment models and fee-splitting arrangements
Electronic health record documentation requirements

questions.explanation: The ACR Code of Ethics addresses issues specific to radiology practice, including misleading billing arrangements. Radiologists should not participate in billing arrangements that mislead patients or payers concerning the fees charged. The other answer choices are not ethical considerations.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 1: Core Elements of Professionalism
questions.stem: A radiologist is asked to speak at a conference sponsored by a pharmaceutical company that manufactures contrast agents. According to the ABIM Physician Charter, the most appropriate action is to:

choices.text: Decline all industry-sponsored speaking engagements
Accept only if the talk does not involve contrast agents
Accept without disclosure since speaking fees are standard practice
Disclose the relationship to the audience and ensure content remains unbiased

questions.explanation: The ABIM Physician Charter requires physicians to disclose and manage conflicts of interest. When speaking at industry-sponsored events, full disclosure of the relationship and ensuring unbiased content are the appropriate professional responses.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: Which of the following are the two dimensions of quality?

choices.text: Excellence and Consistency
Accuracy and Efficiency
Excellence and Reliability
Consistency and Compliance

questions.explanation: Quality has two important dimensions: excellence and consistency. It is not enough to provide excellent care; it must be done on a consistent basis. Lack of consistency is a marker of poor quality.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: Which term refers to measuring and testing elements of performance to ensure that standards are met and instances of poor quality are corrected?

choices.text: Quality Improvement (QI)
Quality Assurance (QA)
Continuous Quality Improvement (CQI)
Quality Control (QC)

questions.explanation: Quality control (QC) refers to measuring and testing elements of performance to ensure that standards are met and correcting instances of poor quality. Quality assurance (QA) refers to a process for monitoring and ensuring performance quality in an organization. Quality improvement (QI) refers to activities designed to improve performance quality in an organization in a systematic and sustainable way. As organizations' focus has transitioned in recent decades from seeking to maintain the status quo to seeking to constantly improve performance, the field of quality has transitioned from relying solely on a QA approach to one of continuous quality improvement (CQI).

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a QC activity?

choices.text: Reviewing and correcting errors in a radiology report before finalizing it
Using standardized report templates to minimize errors in reporting
Implementing a program to prevent incorrect aortic imaging protocols, and then tracking the rate at which incorrect protocols are approved
Meeting monthly to identify new opportunities for quality improvement

questions.explanation: Quality control (QC) refers to measuring and testing elements of performance to ensure that standards are met and correcting instances of poor quality. Quality assurance (QA) refers to a process for monitoring and ensuring performance quality in an organization. questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: Which of the following is considered the most basic level of quality-related activities in an organization?

choices.text: Quality control (QC)
Quality assurance (QA)
Quality improvement (QI)
Continuous quality improvement (CQI)

questions.explanation: QC is generally considered to be the most basic level of quality-related activities in an organization. QA is more comprehensive than QC and is required to maintain consistently high-performance levels in an organization. QI assumes that quality is not as good as it could be and employs strategies to successfully improve quality through a variety of means, including changes in processes, systems, and even organizational structure.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: The ongoing, dynamic process of identifying opportunities and implementing changes to improve quality is best described as:

choices.text: Continuous Quality Improvement
Quality Control
Quality Assurance
Root Cause Analysis

questions.explanation: Continuous Quality Improvement (CQI) is an ongoing, iterative process that continuously identifies and implements incremental improvements. It is contrasted with QA, which focuses primarily on monitoring against fixed standards.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: The IOM report 'Crossing the Quality Chasm' (2001) defined six aims for health care quality. Which of the following is NOT one of those aims?

choices.text: Safe
Effective
Equitable
Preventive

questions.explanation: The six aims of 'Crossing the Quality Chasm' are: Safe, Effective, Patient-centered, Timely, Efficient, and Equitable (STEEEP). Preventive is not among them, though it may sound plausible.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: Which of the following accurately lists the six aims of healthcare quality, as outlined by the IOM report 'Crossing the Quality Chasm'?

choices.text: Secure, Effective, Professional, Timely, Efficient, and Equitable
Safe, Effective, Patient-centered, Trustworthy, Efficient, and Equitable
Sensible, Effective, Preventive, Trustworthy, Efficient, and Equitable
Safe, Effective, Patient-centered, Timely, Efficient, and Equitable

questions.explanation: The six aims of 'Crossing the Quality Chasm' are: Safe, Effective, Patient-centered, Timely, Efficient, and Equitable (STEEEP).

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: The IOM 'Crossing the Quality Chasm' report described the 'quality chasm' as the gap between:

choices.text: Public and private healthcare delivery systems
The care patients receive and the care they should receive
Urban and rural healthcare access and infrastructure
Experienced and novice physicians in clinical performance

questions.explanation: The 'quality chasm' refers to the serious, pervasive gap between the care that Americans actually receive and the care that they could and should receive based on available scientific knowledge.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT represent a core competency of the ABMS AND ACGME?

choices.text: Managing conflicts of interest
Practice-based learning and improvement
Systems-based practice
Patient-care and procedural skills

questions.explanation: Managing conflicts of interest is a professional responsibility of physicians. All the other answer choices represent core competencies.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: The landmark IOM report 'To Err is Human' estimated that medical errors caused approximately how many preventable deaths annually in the United States?
questions.explanation: 'To Err is Human' (IOM, 2000) estimated that between 44,000 and 98,000 Americans die each year as a result of medical errors, making it a leading cause of death. This report catalyzed the patient safety movement.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: What is the projected societal cost of medical errors?

choices.text: $200 million
$2 billion
$200 billion
$20 billion

questions.explanation: 'To Err is Human' (IOM, 2000) projected total societal costs of medical errors to be between $17 billion and $29 billion.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: According to the 2000 IOM report 'To Err is Human', which of the following is NOT identified as a fundamental factor contributing to medical errors?

choices.text: The decentralized nature of the healthcare delivery system
The failure of licensing systems to focus on identifying errors
The failure of individual practitioners to maintain sufficient medical knowledge and skills
The failure of third-party providers to provide financial incentive to improve safety

questions.explanation: The report identified four fundamental contributing factors: (1) the decentralized nature of the healthcare delivery system, (2) the failure of licensing systems to focus on errors, (3) the impediment of the liability system to identify errors, and (4) the failure of third-party providers to provide financial incentive to improve safety. Notably, the report emphasized that most errors stem from unsafe systems and processes rather than individual practitioner failures - making option C a plausible but incorrect choice, as the report explicitly argues against "rooting out bad apples" as a viable strategy.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: According to the 2015 IOM report 'Improving Diagnosis in Health Care', which of the following is NOT among the recommendations made for IT professionals and organizational leaders to improve communication?

choices.text: Standardize communication policies and definitions across networked organizations
Implement effective results management and tracking processes within clinical systems
Develop shared quality and reporting metrics among participating organizations
Establish mandatory peer review processes for all diagnostic imaging interpretations

questions.explanation: The 2015 IOM report made four specific recommendations for IT professionals and organizational leaders: (1) standardize communication policies and definitions across networked organizations, (2) ensure clear identification of the patient's care team to facilitate contact by the radiology team, (3) implement effective results management and tracking processes, and (4) develop shared quality and reporting metrics. Mandatory peer review of imaging interpretations, while a reasonable quality improvement concept discussed elsewhere in radiology practice, was not listed among these communication-focused recommendations.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of human factors engineering?

choices.text: Requiring additional training and coaching sessions for physicians who commit knowledge-based errors
Using checklists to ensure that safety steps are performed and completed in the correct order
Providing increased supervision for healthcare providers working in high-acuity clinical environments
Implementing deliberate practice programs to reduce recurring procedural errors among clinical staff

questions.explanation: Using checklists to ensure safety steps are performed in the correct order is a foundational example of human factors engineering, which focuses on designing systems that account for human strengths and limitations to optimize safety and minimize error. While the other three options are all legitimate error-reduction strategies, they are not examples of human factors engineering. Additional training and coaching (A), increased supervision (C), and deliberate practice (D) are strategies suited to rules- and knowledge-based errors. Notably, additional training is generally less effective for skill-based errors - precisely the context where human factors engineering interventions, such as behavior-shaping system design, are most impactful.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: A radiologist calls the referring clinician to communicate a critical imaging finding. After relaying the results, the radiologist asks the clinician to repeat the information back to confirm understanding. This read-back technique best represents which component of communication?

choices.text: Conveyance, as it involves the transmission of information from one party to another
Convergence, as it involves verification and clarification until both parties agree on the meaning of the information
Convergence, as it involves the initial transmission of findings from the radiologist to the referring team
Conveyance, as it confirms that the message was successfully received and interpreted by the listener

questions.explanation: Communication consists of two components: conveyance - the transmission of information from sender to receiver - and convergence - the verification, discussion, and clarification until both parties recognize that they mutually agree on the meaning. The read-back technique is a classic convergence activity, and convergence is considered especially critical when information is ambiguous or when the consequences of miscommunication are severe. Option D incorrectly labels this activity as conveyance, which refers only to the initial transmission, not the confirmation of shared understanding.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: Which of the following best characterizes a high-reliability organization (HRO)?

choices.text: An organization that eliminates human error entirely through strict individual accountability and disciplinary protocols
An organization that limits operational complexity by standardizing all clinical workflows to achieve consistent performance
An organization that manages a complex environment to achieve the fewest number of errors
An organization that relies primarily on individual expertise and advanced training to prevent adverse events

questions.explanation: An HRO is defined not by the absence of risk, but by its ability to maintain safety despite operating in a high-stress, high-risk, complex environment. HROs accomplish this through mindful management of their environment and a constant state of vigilance. Options A and D place disproportionate emphasis on individual-level solutions, which is inconsistent with the systems-based approach that defines HROs. Option B mischaracterizes the concept by focusing on simplification rather than mindful management of complexity.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly identifies all three elements of anticipation in a high-reliability organization?

choices.text: Commitment to resilience, reluctance to simplify, and deference to expertise
Preoccupation with failure, sensitivity to operations, and commitment to resilience
Preoccupation with failure, reluctance to simplify, and sensitivity to operations
Deference to expertise, preoccupation with failure, and reluctance to simplify

questions.explanation: HROs maintain resilience through two overarching strategies: anticipation and containment. Anticipation has three elements - preoccupation with failure, reluctance to simplify, and sensitivity to operations. Commitment to resilience and deference to expertise are the two elements of containment, not anticipation. Options A, B, and D each mix elements from both categories.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: A radiology department routinely investigates minor dictation errors and near-miss contrast reactions with the same rigor applied to serious adverse events. This practice best reflects which element of anticipation in an HRO?

choices.text: Reluctance to simplify
Sensitivity to operations
Preoccupation with failure
Commitment to resilience

questions.explanation: Preoccupation with failure describes an organizational mindset in which even minor lapses are recognized as potentially harboring severe consequences, prompting deliberate vigilance for early warning signs. The department's practice of rigorously investigating small errors reflects exactly this mindset. Reluctance to simplify (A) refers to digging deeper into the root cause rather than accepting surface-level explanations. Sensitivity to operations (B) refers to leadership's awareness of what is actually happening on the ground versus what is supposed to be happening. Commitment to resilience (D) is an element of containment, not anticipation.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: A junior radiology technologist raises a concern about a potential equipment malfunction during a procedure. Despite being the least senior person in the room, her concern is promptly acted upon by the attending radiologist. This interaction best exemplifies which element of containment in a high-reliability organization?

choices.text: Sensitivity to operations
Commitment to resilience
Deference to expertise
Preoccupation with failure

questions.explanation: Deference to expertise recognizes that people with greater authority often have less useful situational knowledge than those with lesser authority. HROs overcome the dangers of hierarchy by enabling leaders to defer to the relevant expertise regardless of its source, while preserving the organizational structure. Commitment to resilience (B) refers to empowering individuals to adjust and learn from unexpected events after they occur - a related but distinct concept. Options A and D describe elements of anticipation, not containment.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: A radiologist is dictating a report on a study he has read hundreds of times before. Despite correctly identifying the finding on the image, he inadvertently dictates the wrong anatomical side. This type of error is best classified as:

choices.text: A knowledge-based error
A rules-based error
A skill-based error
A convergence failure

questions.explanation: Skill-based actions are those performed largely automatically, requiring little conscious attention - such as driving on an open freeway or, in this case, routine dictation. Errors in this cognitive mode tend to be slips rather than reflections of knowledge or rule deficits. Knowledge-based errors (A) arise in novel situations requiring high concentration. Rules-based errors (B) occur at an intermediate level of attention during familiar decision-making tasks. Convergence failure (D) is a component of communication breakdown, not a classification of human error type.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate management strategy for a skill-based error committed by a radiologist?

choices.text: Providing additional training and coaching to address the underlying knowledge deficit
Counseling the individual and offering better incentives for correct performance
Redesigning the system or workflow to reduce the likelihood of the error recurring
Increasing supervisory oversight until the radiologist demonstrates improved performance

questions.explanation: Skill-based errors are best addressed through behavior-shaping constraints and system redesign - interventions that make the wrong action harder to perform or the right action easier. Additional training (A) is generally less effective for skill-based errors because the problem is not a knowledge gap but rather an automatic action that bypasses conscious attention. Counseling and incentivizing (B) are strategies suited to at-risk behavior in the Just Culture model. Increased supervision (D) is more applicable to rules- and knowledge-based errors.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT identified by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) as a key feature of a culture of safety?

choices.text: A blame-free environment where individuals can report errors or near misses without fear of reprimand or punishment
Encouragement of collaboration across ranks and disciplines to seek solutions to patient safety problems
Organizational commitment of resources to address safety concerns
A zero-tolerance disciplinary framework applied uniformly to all safety violations regardless of intent or context

questions.explanation: The AHRQ identifies four key features of a culture of safety: acknowledgment of the high-risk nature of the organization's activities, a blame-free environment for reporting errors, encouragement of cross-disciplinary collaboration, and organizational commitment of resources to safety. A zero-tolerance policy applied without regard to intent or context is inconsistent with the blame-free, non-punitive philosophy central to safety culture. This type of indiscriminate punitive approach is more characteristic of the traditional blame culture that safety culture frameworks seek to replace.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: A radiology department has a culture in which technologists and trainees rarely voice safety concerns to senior radiologists for fear of appearing incompetent or inviting criticism. Which of the following is the most likely consequence of this steep authority gradient?

choices.text: Improved safety outcomes
More accurate measurement of error rates
Underreporting of safety problems
Stronger organizational resilience

questions.explanation: Steep authority gradients - particularly in environments where there is fear of punishment - result in safety problems being rarely reported to senior leadership. This not only undermines the safety culture but also increases the difficulty of accurately measuring error rates, as the true frequency of adverse events becomes hidden.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: Under the Just Culture model, which of the following best defines "at-risk behavior"?

choices.text: An unintentional error that is a product of the current system design and behavioral choices
A choice in which the risk is believed to be insignificant or justified
A conscious disregard for a substantial risk
An unavoidable human lapse in a high-stress environment

questions.explanation: At-risk behavior is defined as a choice where the risk is believed to be insignificant or justified - such as failing to communicate a critical result because the individual underestimates its urgency. The recommended response is to counsel the individual and coach them toward better behavior. Option A describes human error, for which the recommended approach is to console and address system-level factors. Option C describes reckless behavior, for which punitive action is appropriate. Option D also describes human error and conflates it with the at-risk category.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: An anesthesiologist makes a critical dosing error while managing an unfamiliar clinical scenario under time pressure, resulting in a patient death. The most appropriate institutional response is to:

choices.text: Punish the physician, as the patient was harmed and accountability must be maintained
Coach the physician and provide better incentives to prevent similar decisions in the future
Console the physician and focus improvement efforts on the system design and workflows that contributed to the error
Remediate or remove the physician from clinical duties pending a formal investigation into reckless conduct

questions.explanation: Under the Just Culture model, the response to an error is based on the type of behavior involved, not the outcome or severity of harm. This scenario describes a human error - an unintentional mistake arising from an unfamiliar situation, not a conscious disregard for safety rules. Human errors are best addressed by consoling the individual and directing improvement efforts at the system and workflow factors that made the error possible. Punitive action (A and D) is reserved for reckless behavior. Coaching (B) is the appropriate response to at-risk behavior, not human error.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: A radiology resident is reviewing an abdominal CT that displays a pattern he has encountered many times before. Recognizing it as familiar, he applies his standard interpretive approach without pausing to consider the patient's unique clinical history, and recommends a follow-up strategy appropriate for a common benign process. The finding ultimately proves to represent a malignancy requiring a different management pathway. This error is best classified as:

choices.text: Skill-based error
Rules-based error
Knowledge-based error
At-risk behavior

questions.explanation: Rules-based actions require an intermediate level of attention and involve applying familiar patterns or protocols to situations that appear routine. This resident recognized a familiar pattern and applied an associated rule - but did so incorrectly. A skill-based error (A) would involve a largely automatic action with little conscious engagement, such as a dictation slip. A knowledge-based error (C) arises when a situation is genuinely novel and requires reasoning from first principles - here, the resident was applying a familiar rule, not encountering an unknown clinical scenario. At-risk behavior (D) is a Just Culture behavioral category, not a cognitive error classification under the SRK model.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: A senior radiology fellow is asked to evaluate a chest CT in a patient with a rare autoimmune condition presenting with an atypical imaging pattern she has never encountered during training. Despite careful and concentrated analysis, she arrives at an incorrect diagnosis. This error is best classified as:

choices.text: Skill-based error
Rules-based error
Knowledge-based error
Reckless behavior

questions.explanation: Knowledge-based actions require a high level of concentration and occur in situations that are new or unfamiliar to the individual - analogous to driving in poor visibility conditions in an unfamiliar city for the first time. The fellow is reasoning from first principles in an entirely novel clinical context, which is the defining feature of the knowledge-based cognitive mode. Skill-based errors (A) involve automatic, low-attention actions. Rules-based errors (B) involve misapplication of a familiar pattern to a case that appears routine - the fellow here had no applicable familiar framework to misapply. Reckless behavior (D) requires conscious disregard for a known and substantial risk, which is absent in this scenario.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: A safety framework that balances the need to reduce blame with the need to maintain individual accountability best describes which of the following concepts?

choices.text: Culture of safety
Blame-free environment
High-reliability organization
Just culture

questions.explanation: Just culture, proposed by David Marx, is specifically designed to resolve the tension between a blame-free approach and individual accountability by tailoring the institutional response to the nature of the behavior - not the outcome. A culture of safety (A) is a broader AHRQ-defined organizational concept with multiple features, of which just culture is one component. A blame-free environment (B) captures only part of the just culture framework - just culture goes further by preserving accountability for at-risk and reckless behaviors. A high-reliability organization (C) is a systems-level concept centered on mindful management of complex, high-risk environments. Deference to expertise (E) is an element of containment within HROs, unrelated to accountability frameworks.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: A radiologist routinely documents critical imaging findings in the electronic health record without placing a direct phone call to the ordering clinician, believing that electronic notification is sufficient and that a phone call merely duplicates information already captured in the record. This behavior is best classified as:

choices.text: Human error
At-risk behavior
Reckless behavior
Skill-based error

questions.explanation: At-risk behavior is defined as a choice in which the risk is believed to be insignificant or justified - precisely the reasoning this radiologist is applying. Failing to directly communicate critical results in favor of a workaround of convenience is offered in the study guide as a prototypical example of at-risk behavior that could subvert established safety precautions. The key distinction from reckless behavior (C) is that the radiologist genuinely believes the alternative is adequate, making coaching the appropriate response rather than punitive action. Human error (A) would apply if the deviation were unintentional rather than a deliberate choice. A skill-based error (D) is a cognitive error classification under the SRK model, not a Just Culture behavioral category.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 2: Core Concepts of Quality and Safety
questions.stem: An attending interventional radiologist refuses to perform pre-procedure "time-outs", dismissing them as unnecessary formalities for experienced practitioners. The most appropriate institutional response is:

choices.text: Console the attending and focus improvement efforts on redesigning the preprocedural verification workflow
Coach the attending and modify training programs to reinforce the importance of preprocedural safety steps
Remediate or remove the attending from the procedural environment and take punitive action as warranted
Implement behavior-shaping constraints to make it harder for any team member to bypass the verification steps

questions.explanation: This scenario describes reckless behavior - a conscious disregard for a substantial and unjustifiable risk - characterized by willful, repeated violation of firmly established safety protocols, compounded by prior counseling that has failed to change the behavior. Consoling and system redesign (A) are strategies reserved for human error, where system factors are primarily implicated. Coaching (B) is the appropriate response to at-risk behavior, where the individual underestimates risk - not for behavior that reflects deliberate and repeated disregard for known safety standards. Behavior-shaping constraints (D) are a human factors engineering approach best suited to skill-based errors, not willful noncompliance.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: What is the primary objective of a daily management system (DMS)?

choices.text: To facilitate communication and coordination within and across organizational units and roles on a continuous basis
To provide a structured framework for conducting dedicated improvement projects in areas requiring focused effort
To establish standardized performance metrics for measuring quality and safety across a department
To identify and resolve complex systemic problems that cannot be addressed through routine clinical workflows

questions.explanation: A daily management system provides a day-to-day operating framework for leaders to engage with staff to solve problems on a continuous basis. Its objective is specifically to facilitate communication and coordination within and across organizational units and roles. Option B describes project-based improvement methods, which are a separate category of quality improvement activity suited to problems too difficult to solve with routine daily methods. Options C and D describe activities that may occur within a DMS but are not its defining objective.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a "huddle" in the context of a daily management system?

choices.text: A formal monthly meeting of department leaders to review quarterly performance dashboards
A brief structured meeting in which participants review what has recently occurred, the current status of the unit, and what is anticipated in the near future
A dedicated problem-solving session convened to investigate a specific adverse event or near miss
A weekly interdepartmental meeting between frontline staff and executive leadership to address safety concerns

questions.explanation: A huddle is defined as a brief structured meeting occurring in an organizational unit in which participants review what has recently occurred, the current status of the unit, and what is anticipated in the near future. First-tier huddles are held within local units, with unit leaders attending higher-tier huddles in a cascading structure up to the executive team. The other options describe less frequent or more formal meetings that do not match the brief, continuous nature of a daily huddle.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: At the start of each shift, a radiology department team reviews whether all imaging equipment is operational, confirms that appropriate staff are in place to meet patient needs, verifies that necessary supplies are stocked, and ensures that proper protocols are available for any patients with special needs. This activity best represents which component of a daily management system?

choices.text: Problem management and accountability cycle
Goal and metrics review
Daily readiness assessment
Tiered huddle

questions.explanation: A daily readiness assessment helps staff determine whether they are prepared to accommodate the number and types of patients expected that day. The four topics typically reviewed are: methods (ensuring proper protocols are in place), equipment (confirming operational status and staff training), supplies (ensuring availability), and associates (confirming appropriate staffing). The problem management and accountability cycle (A) focuses on ongoing tracking of identified problems. Goal and metrics review (B) involves reviewing quantitative performance data. A tiered huddle (D) is the broader meeting structure within which a readiness assessment may be conducted but is not the assessment itself.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the role of a visibility board in a daily management system?

choices.text: To easily display departmental performance metrics
To track important elements of the daily management huddles for all staff members to see
To communicate patient census and anticipated workflow demands
To record adverse events and near misses for review at monthly safety meetings

questions.explanation: A visibility board is described as often simply an organized whiteboard that tracks important elements of the daily management huddles for all staff members to see. Problems identified at the huddle are documented on the visibility board along with the owner of the problem and the expected resolution date, supporting the problem management and accountability cycle. It is a shared, visible tool - not restricted to administrators as in option A - and is distinct from scheduling tools or adverse event reporting systems.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the role of the project sponsor in a quality improvement project?

choices.text: Directing the day-to-day activities of the project
Providing organizational oversight and support
Advising and supporting the team on improvement methodology
Contributing frontline knowledge of the processes being studied

questions.explanation: The project sponsor provides organizational oversight and support, removes barriers as they arise, and has the organizational authority to provide resources and resolve interpersonal conflicts. Importantly, while sponsors may offer general guidance, they should avoid overstepping their bounds and assuming the project leader's role. Option A describes the project leader's role. Option C describes the project coach. Option D describes the role of project participants.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the role of the project leader in a quality improvement project?

choices.text: Providing organizational authority to remove barriers, secure resources, and resolve conflicts that arise during the project
Directing and coordinating project activities
Advising the team on quality improvement methodology
Contributing daily operational knowledge of the targeted process

questions.explanation: The project leader directs and coordinates project activities to ensure success, assembles the team, manages the project, delegates and follows up on assignments, reports progress, alerts the sponsor when more help is needed, and ensures timely completion. Project leaders should have strong organizational and leadership skills. Option A describes the project sponsor. Option C describes the project coach. Option D describes the project participants.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the ideal composition of project participants in a quality improvement project?

choices.text: Department administrators
Frontline staff
Subject matter experts
Senior organizational leaders

questions.explanation: Project participants should be selected from the areas targeted for improvement, with each organizational unit included in the targeted process represented on the team. It is generally more effective to select frontline staff who perform the work on a daily basis, rather than supervisors, managers, or other organizational leaders. Participation should be voluntary. Option C describes the project coach. Options A and D more closely resemble characteristics of a project sponsor.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the role of the project coach in a quality improvement project?

choices.text: Providing organizational authority to secure resources and remove barriers
Directing and coordinating day-to-day project activities
An expert in improvement methods who advises and supports the team
A frontline representative who contributes daily operational knowledge of the process targeted for improvement

questions.explanation: The project coach is an expert in improvement methods who advises and supports the team, helps guide the project leader, facilitates communication with the sponsor, and alerts organizational leaders when the project appears to be off track. Critically, the coach should avoid encroaching on the role of the project leader or performing tasks belonging to project participants. Option A describes the project sponsor. Option B describes the project leader. Option D describes project participants.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A quality improvement team is tracking outcomes of a new contrast reaction protocol. Which of the following would be classified as an end outcome measure?

choices.text: Adherence rate to the new contrast administration checklist
Mean time from contrast reaction onset to treatment administration
Supply utilization rate for emergency contrast reaction medications
Rate of patient morbidity attributable to contrast reactions

questions.explanation: End outcomes are the broadest category of outcome measures and include morbidity, patient satisfaction, and costs. Morbidity - such as the rate of patient harm attributable to contrast reactions - is a prototypical end outcome. Adherence to a checklist (A) is a process measure. Mean treatment response time (B) and supply utilization (C) are intermediate outcomes, which reflect service times and resource utilization rather than the final impact on the patient.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of an intermediate outcome measure?

choices.text: Total cost of imaging per patient encounter
The rate at which an incorrect exam protocol had to be corrected
Patient satisfaction with the radiology experience
Adherence to the standard contrast injection protocol

questions.explanation: Intermediate outcomes include service times, error rates, and supply utilization - measures that reflect performance within the care process but sit between process-level activities and final patient outcomes. Costs (A) and patient satisfaction (C) are end outcomes. Adherence to a protocol (D) is a process measure, as it reflects whether a specific step in the workflow was performed as intended.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a process measure?

choices.text: Rate of contrast-induced nephropathy following CT angiography
Patient-reported satisfaction with radiology staff communication
Time required to complete each step of the patient check-in workflow
Rate of wrong-patient imaging events per 1,000 examinations

questions.explanation: Process measures assess performance at the level of individual steps within a workflow, such as times for each process step, adherence to standard work, and equipment utilization rates. Time to complete each step of the check-in process directly measures process-level performance. Contrast-induced nephropathy (A) and wrong-patient events (D) are end outcomes reflecting patient harm. Patient satisfaction (B) is also an end outcome.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A quality improvement team tracking mean daily CT turnaround time creates a graph plotting data points over several months. The graph displays the mean before the project began, the mean at the project's conclusion, and the performance goal - and also includes numbered markers identifying the specific dates and descriptions of each intervention that was implemented. This is best described as:

choices.text: A Pareto chart
A run chart
An annotated run chart
A fishbone diagram

questions.explanation: An annotated run chart is a run chart that also indicates the dates and nature of interventions implemented during the project. A standard run chart (B) displays data over time with the mean and performance goal but does not include annotations for specific interventions. A Pareto chart (A) displays the frequency of problem causes ranked from most to least common. A fishbone diagram (D) documents and categorizes the potential causes of a problem.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A standard run chart used to monitor performance during a quality improvement project should display which of the following?

choices.text: The mean performance level during the active project period
The mean before the beginning of the project, the mean at the end of the project, and the performance goal
Individual data points over time, with annotated markers indicating the dates and nature of each intervention
The frequency distribution of problem causes ranked from most to least common

questions.explanation: A run chart should display the mean before the beginning of the project, the mean at the end of the project, and the performance goal. Showing only the mean during the active project period (A) would obscure the baseline against which improvement is measured. Option C describes an annotated run chart, which is a specific subtype of run chart. Option D describes a Pareto chart.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A radiology department sets the following improvement goal: "Our goal is to decrease mean daily examination completion time from 120 minutes to 30 minutes by July 1, 2026." Which attribute of the SMART framework is best illustrated by the inclusion of the phrase "by July 1, 2026"?

choices.text: Specific
Measurable
Relevant
Time-bound

questions.explanation: SMART goals should be specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound. Including a target date ("by July 1, 2026") satisfies the time-bound criterion. The numerical values (from 120 to 30 minutes) address the specific and measurable criteria. Relevance (C) pertains to whether the goal aligns with the organization's values and priorities - a judgment that cannot be assessed from the date component alone.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: Which of the following goal statements is LEAST consistent with the SMART framework?

choices.text: "Reduce mean CT report turnaround time from 45 minutes to 20 minutes by December 31, 2026"
"Improve the overall quality of radiology reports across the department"
"Decrease the rate of wrong-patient imaging events from 3 per month to 0 per month by June 30, 2026"
"Reduce mean fluoroscopy procedure time from 18 minutes to 12 minutes by March 1, 2026"

questions.explanation: A SMART goal must state the beginning performance, the end performance, and the date - "from what, to what, by when." Option B is vague, lacks a numerical baseline and target, and provides no timeframe, failing to meet the specific, measurable, and time-bound criteria simultaneously. Options A, C, and D all identify a clear starting point, a target, and a deadline, fulfilling the core structural requirements of the SMART framework.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A quality improvement team investigating the over-ordering of CT scans in the emergency department creates a diagram that organizes potential contributing causes into categories including people, policies and practice, materials and technology, and processes/procedures - all pointing toward the identified problem. This tool is best described as:

choices.text: A Pareto chart
A run chart
A cause-and-effect diagram
A PDSA planning worksheet

questions.explanation: A cause-and-effect diagram, also known as a fishbone diagram, is used to document and categorize the potential causes of a problem that negatively impacts performance. Categories such as people, policies and practice, materials and technology, and processes/procedures are depicted along the "bones" of the diagram, converging on the identified problem - the "effect." A Pareto chart (A) is used after causes have been identified to display their relative frequency. A run chart (B) tracks performance over time.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: The Pareto principle, also known as the "80/20 rule," states which of the following?

choices.text: Eighty percent of improvement projects fail without executive sponsorship
A small number of causes are usually responsible for the majority of problems
At least 80% of errors in a complex system can be attributed to individual human failure
The majority of problems in a system are caused by a large number of equally distributed contributing factors

questions.explanation: The Pareto principle states that a few causes are usually responsible for the majority of problems. This principle guides teams to prioritize their problem-solving efforts toward the highest-frequency contributors rather than attempting to address all identified causes simultaneously. Option D is the direct opposite of the Pareto principle. Options A and C are not supported by this framework.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: After documenting the frequency of various causes of inappropriate emergency department imaging orders using a tally sheet, a quality improvement team plots these causes in a bar graph ranked in descending order of frequency. This display is best described as a:

choices.text: Run chart
Fishbone diagram
Pareto chart
PDSA planning diagram

questions.explanation: A Pareto chart illustrates which causes occur most frequently, enabling the team to prioritize problem-solving efforts toward the most impactful contributors. The tally sheet is the tool used to collect raw frequency data; the Pareto chart then displays those frequencies in descending order to make priorities visually apparent. A fishbone diagram (B) is used earlier in the process to identify and categorize potential causes before their frequency has been measured. An annotated run chart (A) tracks performance over time with intervention markers.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: The PDSA cycle is a method for iteratively testing, refining, and validating process changes. What does the acronym PDSA stand for?

choices.text: Plan, Deploy, Standardize, Assess
Plan, Do, Study, Act
Prepare, Design, Sustain, Analyze
Problem, Define, Solve, Assess

questions.explanation: PDSA stands for Plan, Do, Study, Act. The cycle is essentially a restatement of the scientific method and can be thought of as a planned test of change. Each step corresponds to a phase of iterative testing: developing a plan, executing the test, analyzing the results, and determining next steps. The other options are plausible-sounding acronym expansions but do not reflect the actual framework.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A quality improvement team hypothesizes that placing a patient-ready form in the technologist's inbox will reduce mean examination completion time. They design a small-scale two-week trial on a single unit, define what data will be collected, and specify in advance how success will be measured. Which step of the PDSA cycle does this activity best represent?

choices.text: Plan
Do
Study
Act

questions.explanation: The Plan step involves developing a plan to test the hypothesis of how a process change will lead to a desired outcome. Designing the trial, defining the intervention, and specifying data collection methods are all planning activities. The Do step involves actually executing the test. The Study step involves analyzing the resulting data. The Act step involves drawing actionable conclusions and deciding whether to adopt, modify, or abandon the intervention.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: After implementing an electronic alert on technologist workscreens, a quality improvement team reviews the collected data and finds that examination completion times improved on day shifts but not on evening shifts. They conclude the intervention requires modification and decide to add a secondary alert for evening staff before testing again on a broader scale. Which steps of the PDSA cycle do these two activities - reviewing the data and determining the next course of action - best represent?

choices.text: Plan and Do
Do and Study
Study and Act
Act and Plan

questions.explanation: Analyzing the collected data corresponds to the Study step, in which the team objectively evaluates whether the intervention achieved the desired outcome. Drawing actionable conclusions and determining next steps - here, modifying the intervention for retesting - corresponds to the Act step. Together, Study and Act represent the reflective back half of the PDSA cycle. It is expected that many proposed changes will be unsuccessful in their initial form and will require revision before full implementation.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A radiology department successfully reduces its mean CT turnaround time through a quality improvement project but discontinues active monitoring after the project concludes. Six months later, performance has returned to pre-project levels. This outcome is best explained by which of the following?

choices.text: Without deliberate mechanisms to sustain improvements, performance typically reverts to the initial state
The PDSA cycles were not executed on a sufficiently large scale to produce durable change
The project goal was not SMART, leading to ambiguous targets that staff could not maintain
Frontline staff were not adequately represented among the project participants

questions.explanation: Without deliberate mechanisms to sustain improvements, performance usually reverts to the initial state. Strategies to counteract this include establishing regular measurement and feedback, using handoffs to enforce standards, establishing the practice of stopping the process when a problem is encountered, embedding checks into the process, and using high-reliability solutions. The scenario specifically describes the absence of ongoing monitoring - the most direct driver of reversion described in the framework.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A radiology department is evaluating strategies to sustain a reduction in contrast extravasation rates. Ranked from LEAST TO MOST reliable in terms of consistency of outcome, which of the following correctly orders these sustaining strategies?

choices.text: Infrastructure redesign → standardization of procedures → education and feedback
Standardization of procedures → education and feedback → infrastructure redesign
Education and feedback → standardization of procedures → infrastructure redesign
Education and feedback → infrastructure redesign → standardization of procedures

questions.explanation: In the hierarchy of high-reliability solutions, processes that rely on education and feedback tend to result in the lowest consistency of outcome. Standardization of procedures produces greater reliability than education and feedback. Changes to infrastructure and organizational culture result in the highest consistency of outcome and require the least effort by the process owner to sustain. As a general rule, high-reliability process changes are more effective and require less ongoing effort to maintain than low-reliability solutions such as training programs alone.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: According to patient safety guidelines, what is the minimum number of identifiers that should be confirmed before performing a procedure?

choices.text: Two
One
Three
Four

questions.explanation: At least two patient identifiers should be confirmed before every procedure, including before medication administration, invasive or noninvasive procedures, and blood product administration. This requirement also serves to reduce the chance of unnecessary radiation exposure. Using two identifiers provides redundancy that a single identifier cannot.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: Which of the following may NOT be used as a patient identifier prior to a procedure?

choices.text: Date of birth
Assigned identification number
Patient's room number or location within the facility
Last four digits of the social security number

questions.explanation: Transient factors such as a patient's room number or location within the facility cannot be used as identifiers, because they can change and are not person-specific. Valid identifiers include patient name, assigned identification number, telephone number, date of birth, government-issued photo identification, and the last four digits of the social security number.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as an element that should be assessed and documented prior to initiating sedation?

choices.text: Recent oral intake and recent illness
Pulmonary status, including upper airway assessment
Review of recent imaging
Baseline vital signs and level of consciousness

questions.explanation: Before sedation is initiated, the required clinical assessment elements include recent oral intake, recent illness, pulmonary status (including upper airway), cardiac status, baseline vital signs, level of consciousness, pulse oximetry, capnography (if available), and electrocardiography when applicable. Imaging review not part of the clinical presedation assessment.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A patient undergoing a CT-guided procedure receives an anxiolytic medication prior to the start of the case. She responds normally to verbal commands throughout the procedure. Her cognitive function and coordination are mildly impaired. Ventilatory and cardiovascular functions remain completely unaffected. Which level of sedation does this best describe?

choices.text: Moderate sedation
Minimal sedation
Deep sedation
General anesthesia

questions.explanation: Minimal sedation/anxiolysis is a drug-induced state in which the patient responds normally to verbal commands. While cognitive function and coordination may be impaired, ventilatory and cardiovascular functions remain specifically unaffected - this is the key feature distinguishing minimal sedation from deeper levels. At the moderate sedation level (A), the patient has a mildly depressed level of consciousness but retains protective reflexes and can be aroused by physical or verbal stimulation. At the deep sedation level (C), the patient cannot be easily aroused and independent ventilatory function may be compromised. General anesthesia (D) involves controlled unconsciousness with complete loss of protective airway reflexes.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A patient undergoing a radiology procedure achieves a mildly depressed level of consciousness following pharmacologic administration. She retains a continuous and independent ability to maintain a patent airway and protective reflexes, and can be aroused by physical or verbal stimulation. Which level of sedation does this best describe?

choices.text: Moderate sedation
Minimal sedation
Deep sedation
General anesthesia

questions.explanation: Moderate sedation/analgesia is defined as a mildly depressed level of consciousness, pharmacologically induced, in which the patient retains a continuous and independent ability to maintain protective reflexes and a patent airway, and can be aroused by physical or verbal stimulation. At the minimal sedation level (B), cognitive function may be impaired but the depth of consciousness depression is less. At the deep sedation level (C), the patient cannot be easily aroused and independent ventilatory function may be compromised.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: During an interventional procedure, a patient cannot be easily aroused but withdraws purposefully after repeated painful stimulation. His respiratory effort appears diminished. Cardiovascular function remains intact. Which level of sedation does this best describe?

choices.text: Minimal sedation
Moderate sedation
Deep sedation
General anesthesia

questions.explanation: Deep sedation/analgesia is a drug-induced depression of consciousness in which the patient cannot be easily aroused but responds purposefully after repeated or painful stimulation. Independent ventilatory function may be impaired and the patient may require assistance maintaining a patent airway, while cardiovascular function is usually maintained. In general anesthesia (D), there is a complete loss of protective reflexes and no appropriate response to painful stimulation.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A patient undergoing an interventional radiology procedure requires pharmacologic induction of unconsciousness. Throughout the case, she is unable to respond to painful stimulation, has lost all protective airway reflexes, and cannot independently maintain a patent airway. Which level of sedation does this best describe?

choices.text: Minimal sedation
Moderate sedation
Deep sedation
General anesthesia

questions.explanation: General anesthesia is a controlled state of unconsciousness characterized by complete loss of protective reflexes - including the ability to independently maintain a patent airway - and inability to respond appropriately to painful stimulation. This distinguishes it from deep sedation (C), in which the patient retains some purposeful response to painful stimulation and cardiovascular function is usually maintained. Moderate sedation (B) is characterized by a mildly depressed level of consciousness with intact protective reflexes. Minimal sedation (A) involves only mild impairment of cognitive function with ventilatory and cardiovascular functions unaffected.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A patient receiving intended moderate sedation during an interventional procedure rapidly progresses to a state in which she can no longer maintain her airway independently and requires ventilatory support. Which of the following is most accurate regarding this clinical situation?

choices.text: The levels of sedation exist on a continuum, and patients may rapidly move to a deeper level than intended
A medication error has occurred, as properly administered moderate sedation prevents this level of respiratory depression
The patient should have been identified as ASA Class V and sedation should not have been initiated by a non-anesthesiologist
This represents an allergic-type reaction to the administered anesthesia agent

questions.explanation: The four levels of sedation are not discrete categories but rather a continuum. Patients may rapidly move between levels and may reach a deeper level of sedation than intended. Because sedation may result in loss of protective reflexes regardless of the intended depth, all sedated patients require monitoring throughout the procedure. This is the fundamental rationale for the monitoring requirements that apply even to minimal or moderate sedation cases.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: Which of the following is listed as a risk factor that should prompt screening of a patient prior to sedation by a non-anesthesiologist?

choices.text: Congestive heart failure
Age greater than 65 years
Prior allergic reaction to iodinated contrast media
Current use of anticoagulant therapy

questions.explanation: Specific risk factors that may increase the likelihood of an adverse outcome from sedation include congenital or acquired abnormalities of the airway, liver failure, lung disease, congestive heart failure, symptomatic brain stem dysfunction, apnea or hypotonia, history of adverse reaction to sedating medications, morbid obesity, and severe gastroesophageal reflux. Age alone, contrast allergy, and anticoagulation are not among the listed sedation-specific risk factors.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as a risk factor for adverse outcomes from sedation administered by a non-anesthesiologist?

choices.text: Morbid obesity
Symptomatic brain stem dysfunction
Severe gastroesophageal reflux
Prior allergic reaction to contrast media

questions.explanation: The listed risk factors include congenital or acquired airway abnormalities, liver failure, lung disease, congestive heart failure, symptomatic brain stem dysfunction, apnea or hypotonia, history of adverse reaction to sedating medications, morbid obesity, and severe gastroesophageal reflux. A prior reaction to contrast media is a relevant preprocedure consideration but is not among the risk factors specifically associated with adverse outcomes from the sedation itself.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A 38-year-old patient presents for an image-guided biopsy. She has well-controlled hypertension managed with a single antihypertensive agent and no other medical problems. What is her most appropriate ASA Physical Status Classification?

choices.text: ASA Class I
ASA Class II
ASA Class III
ASA Class IV

questions.explanation: ASA Class II describes a patient with mild systemic disease. Well-controlled hypertension without end-organ damage is a classic example. ASA Class I (A) is reserved for a normal healthy patient with no systemic disease. ASA Class III (C) would apply if the systemic disease were severe, such as poorly controlled diabetes with end-organ involvement or moderate COPD.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A 72-year-old patient with poorly controlled diabetes, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, and exercise-limiting COPD presents for an interventional procedure. What is the most appropriate ASA Physical Status Classification?

choices.text: ASA Class II
ASA Class III
ASA Class IV
ASA Class V

questions.explanation: ASA Class III describes a patient with severe systemic disease. Multiple poorly controlled or moderate-to-severe chronic conditions that impose functional limitation but do not pose a constant threat to life fall into this category. ASA Class IV (C) would apply if one of these conditions posed a constant threat to life - for example, end-stage heart failure or recent myocardial infarction. ASA Class II (A) describes mild systemic disease.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A patient is admitted to the intensive care unit with end-stage heart failure refractory to maximal medical therapy. What is the most appropriate ASA Physical Status Classification?

choices.text: ASA Class II
ASA Class III
ASA Class IV
ASA Class V

questions.explanation: ASA Class IV describes a patient with severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life. This is distinguished from ASA Class III (B), in which severe systemic disease is present but does not pose an immediate constant threat. ASA Class V (D) is reserved for a moribund patient not expected to survive without the operation itself - a higher level of acuity than described here.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A patient is brought emergently to interventional radiology following a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. What is this patient's ASA Physical Status Classification?

choices.text: ASA Class III
ASA Class IV
ASA Class V
ASA Class VI

questions.explanation: ASA Class V describes a moribund patient who is not expected to survive without the operative intervention. This is distinct from ASA Class IV (B), in which severe systemic disease poses a constant threat to life but the patient is not imminently moribund. ASA Class VI (D) is reserved specifically for declared brain-dead patients whose organs are being removed for donation.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: Which of the following patients should NOT be sedated by a non-anesthesiologist?

choices.text: ASA Class II
ASA Class III
ASA Class IV
ASA Class V

questions.explanation: ASA Class V patients should not be sedated by non-anesthesiologists. Patients in Classes III and IV or with other significant risk factors may require a consultation with anesthesiology or the performance of sedation by an anesthesiologist or anesthetist, but this is not an absolute exclusion from non-anesthesiologist sedation. ASA Class V represents the threshold at which non-anesthesiologist sedation is contraindicated.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: When sedation is performed under the supervision of a radiologist, which of the following personnel requirements must be met?

choices.text: A separate health professional must be present whose focus is to manage monitoring and medications
An anesthesiologist must be present in the room throughout the procedure
A nurse anesthetist must review and cosign the sedation plan prior to medication administration
