Two radiologists must be present - one to perform the procedure and one to oversee sedation management

questions.explanation: When sedation is performed under radiologist supervision, a separate qualified healthcare professional must be present whose primary focus is the monitoring, medicating, and care of the patient. This individual is distinct from the person performing the procedure. The patient must also have intravenous access, and continuous monitoring must include at minimum level of consciousness, respiratory rate, pulse oximetry, blood pressure (as indicated), heart rate, and cardiac rhythm.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A patient who received moderate sedation during an interventional procedure required a reversal agent at the conclusion of the case. The team is evaluating when it is appropriate to discharge the patient. When can the patient be discharged once consciousness and vital signs have been re-established?

choices.text: Immediately
After 30 minutes
After 2 hours
At the discretion of the proceduralist

questions.explanation: The two-hour monitoring period following reversal agent administration exists because the duration of effect of reversal agents may be shorter than that of the sedating agent. This creates a risk of the patient relapsing into a deeper level of sedation after the reversal agent wears off. Options A, B, and D do not account for this pharmacologic risk and would allow premature discharge.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: Which of the following satisfies the requirements of informed consent?

choices.text: A signed consent form
A verbal acknowledgement prior to entering the procedure room
A note in the chart documenting a lengthy discussion with the patient regarding the procedure
A note in the chart from the referring provider document agreement with the intended procedure

questions.explanation: The ACR-SIR Practice Parameter explicitly states that "informed consent is a process and not the simple act of signing a formal document." While a consent form is often used, consent can also be documented through a note in the medical record, a recording, or another permanent modality. The final responsibility for answering the patient's questions and addressing concerns rests with the physician performing or supervising the procedure - not shared equally with the ordering clinician.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a required element of informed consent?

choices.text: The purpose and nature of the intended procedure
Any reasonable alternatives to the proposed procedure
The cost of the procedure
The risks of not proceeding with the proposed procedure

questions.explanation: The six required elements of informed consent are: (1) the purpose and nature of the intended procedure, (2) the method by which the procedure will be performed, (3) likely risks, complications, and expected benefits, (4) risks of not proceeding, (5) any reasonable alternatives to the proposed procedure, and (6) the right to decline the proposed procedure. Financial information is not among the required elements of the consent process.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: An unconscious trauma patient requires emergency embolization for life-threatening hemorrhage. The patient's family has not yet been identified and there is no advance directive on file. How should the team proceed?

choices.text: Proceed without obtaining consent
Proceed once a family member or legal guardian can be reached and consent obtained
Proceed once a two-physician consent waiver is signed
Proceed once medical necessity is documented in the medical record

questions.explanation: An exception to the informed consent process exists when a delay in treatment would jeopardize the health of a patient who is unable to provide consent - such as an unconscious trauma patient for whom family has not yet been identified. Delaying a life-saving procedure to obtain consent in this scenario would itself cause harm and is not required.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A 60-year-old patient with severe dementia requires a CT-guided drainage procedure but lacks the capacity to provide consent. How should the team proceed?

choices.text: Proceed without obtaining consent
Proceed once a family member or legal guardian can be reached and consent obtained
Proceed once a two-physician consent waiver is signed
Proceed once medical necessity is documented in the medical record

questions.explanation: In a non-emergent setting, when a patient cannot give valid consent due to short-term or long-term mental incapacity - whether from medications or otherwise - consent should be obtained from the patient's appointed healthcare representative, legal guardian, or appropriate family member. In emergent settings, consent can be bypassed if a delay in treatment would jeopardize the health of a patient who is unable to provide consent.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: Regarding minors' rights in medical decision-making, which of the following statements is most accurate?

choices.text: Children younger than 18 years cannot make independent medical decisions without consent from a parent or legal guardian
Courts have never allowed children younger than 12 years to make medical decisions and exercise self-determination
Adolescents between ages 14 and 18 are considered legally competent to provide independent informed consent
A minor may provide independent consent only in states that have formally enacted minor consent legislation

questions.explanation: Courts in the United States have never allowed children younger than 12 years to make medical decisions and exercise self-determination. Adolescents between ages 12 and 18 (or 19 in some states) experience a gradual transition to self-determination, influenced by factors including legal determination of maturity, evidence of sufficient decision-making capacity, and conditions that specifically exempt parental consent. Option C is incorrect because decision-making capacity in adolescents is not automatic and depends on the factors described above.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A 15-year-old presents requesting testing and treatment for a suspected sexually transmitted infection. She requests that her parents not be notified. Which of the following best describes the consent framework applicable to this situation?

choices.text: Parental consent may be exempted for conditions including seeking testing or treatment for sexually transmitted diseases
Parental consent is required for patients under 18 regardless of the nature of the condition
The procedure may proceed without parental consent only if two physicians agree that treatment is medically necessary
Independent consent by a minor applies only to emergencies in which parental contact is impossible or would cause a life-threatening delay of care

questions.explanation: Conditions that may exempt parental consent include seeking testing or treatment for sexually transmitted diseases (including HIV), seeking contraception, prenatal care, or abortion, and seeking mental health treatment, emergency care, or treatment of alcohol or drug abuse after the age of 12 years. These exemptions recognize that requiring parental involvement in these specific circumstances may deter minors from seeking necessary care.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: The universal protocol refers to which of the following three-part processes?

choices.text: Preprocedure verification, marking the procedure site, and performing a preprocedure time out
Patient identification, medication verification, and preprocedure time out
Patient assessment, informed consent confirmation, and performing a preprocedure time out
Preprocedure verification, informed consent confirmation, and site marking

questions.explanation: The universal protocol consists of three components: preprocedure verification, marking the procedure site, and performing a preprocedure time out. Notably, site marking may be performed before completing the preprocedure verification. Informed consent and medication verification, while important safety steps, are not components of the universal protocol as defined.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: Which of the following procedures requires site marking prior to the procedure?

choices.text: Upper endoscopy
Umbilical hernia repair
ACL repair
Cardiac catheterization

questions.explanation: A procedure site should be marked at a minimum when there is more than one possible location for the procedure and when performing the procedure in a different location could harm the patient. The patient should be involved in site marking when possible, and the mark must be made by a licensed independent practitioner who will be present when the procedure is performed. The mark should be sufficiently permanent to remain visible after skin preparation and draping. Written alternative processes are appropriate in place of standard site marking for: procedures on mucosal surfaces or the perineum, minimal access procedures treating a lateralized internal organ, interventional procedures in which the catheter or instrument insertion site is not predetermined (such as cardiac catheterization), procedures on teeth, and procedures on premature infants for whom the mark may cause a permanent tattoo.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: For which of the following procedures is an alternative process for site marking most appropriate rather than standard direct marking?

choices.text: CT-guided biopsy of a left adrenal mass
Ultrasound-guided biopsy of a right thyroid nodule
CT-guided drainage of a right pleural effusion
Cardiac catheterization

questions.explanation: Written alternative processes are appropriate in place of standard site marking for: procedures on mucosal surfaces or the perineum, minimal access procedures treating a lateralized internal organ, interventional procedures in which the catheter or instrument insertion site is not predetermined (such as cardiac catheterization), procedures on teeth, and procedures on premature infants for whom the mark may cause a permanent tattoo. The other options all involve procedures with clearly predetermined, lateralized sites where standard marking is applicable.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: During a preprocedure time out, all relevant team members must at a minimum actively communicate and agree upon which of the following?

choices.text: Correct patient identity, medication allergies, and the anesthesia plan
Correct patient identity, correct site, procedure to be done, and estimated procedure duration
Correct patient identity, correct site, procedure to be done, and postprocedure monitoring plan
Correct patient identity, correct site, and procedure to be done

questions.explanation: During the preprocedure time out, all relevant members of the team must at a minimum agree on correct patient identity, correct site, and procedure to be done. The time out should be conducted immediately before the invasive procedure is started or an incision is made, and should involve the individual performing the procedure, anesthesia providers, the circulating nurse, and other active participants. Documentation should be performed according to organizational policy.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: In which of the following situations are alcohol-based hand sanitizers the preferred method of hand hygiene?

choices.text: After known or suspected exposure to Clostridium difficile
After using a restroom
Before eating a meal
When hands are not visibly dirty

questions.explanation: Alcohol-based hand sanitizers are the most effective products for reducing the number of bacteria on the hands and are the preferred method when hands are not visibly dirty. Soap and water is recommended when hands are visibly dirty, before eating, after using a restroom, and after known or suspected exposure to Clostridium difficile, norovirus, or Bacillus anthracis - situations in which alcohol-based sanitizers are insufficient.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A healthcare worker has been providing direct care to a patient with a confirmed Clostridium difficile infection and is about to leave the room. Which hand hygiene method is most appropriate?

choices.text: Alcohol-based hand sanitizer
Any method is acceptable
Surgical hand antisepsis
Soap and water

questions.explanation: Soap and water is specifically recommended after known or suspected exposure to Clostridium difficile, norovirus, or Bacillus anthracis. While alcohol-based sanitizers are the preferred method for general hand decontamination, they are not recommended in these specific situations. The physical washing action of soap and water is important for removing spores that alcohol does not reliably eliminate.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A radiology technologist completes an IV placement, removes his gloves, and is about to proceed to the next patient. Which of the following best describes the appropriate hand hygiene action at this point?

choices.text: Hand hygiene is unnecessary if the gloves remained visibly intact throughout the procedure
Hand hygiene is only required if the technologist will have direct skin contact with the next patient
Hand hygiene should be performed before donning new gloves
Hand hygiene should be performed after glove removal

questions.explanation: Hand hygiene should be performed after glove removal. Gloves do not provide complete protection against hand contamination and should not be used as a substitute for hand hygiene. This is one of the seven specified indications for hand hygiene and applies regardless of whether the gloves appeared intact.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: A radiologist is about to enter a patient's room to perform a physical assessment before a bedside procedure. She has not had any patient contact since she last cleaned her hands. Which of the following best describes the appropriate hand hygiene action?

choices.text: Hand hygiene is not required prior to patient contact if hands appear clean and no patient care has occurred since last hand hygiene
Hand hygiene is required only before performing invasive procedures, not for routine physical assessment
Hand hygiene before patient contact is the responsibility of nursing staff, not the performing physician
Hand hygiene should be performed before and after having direct contact with a patient's skin

questions.explanation: Hand hygiene is specifically required both before and after having direct contact with a patient's skin. This bidirectional requirement protects both the patient from organisms on the provider's hands and the provider from organisms acquired during the encounter.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: During patient care, a technologist finishes managing a wound on a patient's left lower leg and is about to place an IV catheter in the patient's right arm without performing hand hygiene between the two activities. According to hand hygiene guidelines, hand hygiene is required at this point primarily because:

choices.text: Hand hygiene is required before and after every individual patient care task regardless of the body sites involved
Hand hygiene is required when hands will be moving from a contaminated-body site to a clean-body site during patient care
Hand hygiene is required any time a provider transitions between two different anatomical regions of the same patient
Hand hygiene is required after wound care because wound dressings are always considered a source of bloodborne pathogens

questions.explanation: One of the seven specified indications for hand hygiene is when hands will be moving from a contaminated-body site to a clean-body site during patient care. Transitioning from a wound site to an IV placement site on the same patient represents exactly this scenario. While hand hygiene after wound dressing contact (D) is also separately indicated, option B most precisely captures the specific indication that applies to this transition.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: Which of the following scenarios does NOT independently require hand hygiene according to established guidelines?

choices.text: After removing gloves at the conclusion of a contrast injection
After repositioning a patient's pillow during transport
Before eating lunch in the break room
Returning to a reading room workstation after attending a conference in a separate building

questions.explanation: The seven indications for hand hygiene are: before eating, before and after direct contact with a patient's skin, after contact with blood or body fluids, after contact with inanimate objects in the immediate vicinity of the patient, when moving from a contaminated to a clean body site during patient care, after glove removal, and after using a restroom. Returning to a reading room workstation from a conference in a separate building does not meet any of these specific indications. Option B applies because a patient's pillow is an inanimate object in the immediate vicinity of the patient.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: What is the primary goal of a root cause analysis (RCA) following a serious adverse event?

choices.text: To assign individual accountability and determine appropriate disciplinary action for the responsible parties
To create a legally defensible account of the sequence of events
To determine whose actions most directly caused the adverse outcome
To identify both active errors and latent conditions contributing to the event

questions.explanation: Root cause analysis is a structured method used to analyze serious adverse events to decrease the likelihood of recurrence. Its goal is to identify both active errors - occurring at the interface between humans and a complex system - and latent conditions - hidden systemic vulnerabilities that increase the likelihood of adverse events. Serious adverse events are almost never the result of a single cause and are typically associated with numerous contributing factors. RCA is explicitly not designed for individual blame assignment (A or C) or legal documentation (B).

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: During an RCA of a medication error, investigators find that a nurse accidentally administered a full dose of heparin instead of a heparin flush. The investigation further reveals that both vials appear virtually identical and are routinely stocked side by side in the same automated dispenser at the point of care. In this analysis, the near-identical vial appearance and co-location represent which of the following?

choices.text: An active error
A sentinel event
Reckless behavior
A latent condition

questions.explanation: A latent condition is a hidden problem within a healthcare system that increases the likelihood of an adverse event. The near-identical vial appearance and co-location in the same cabinet represent a pre-existing system vulnerability - not an error in and of itself, but a condition that made the active error more likely to occur. The active error is the nurse's act of selecting and administering the wrong medication. RCA is specifically designed to uncover both types of contributors, since addressing only the active error without resolving the latent condition leaves the system vulnerable to recurrence.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 3: Practical Quality and Safety Applications
questions.stem: In the immediate aftermath of a serious contrast reaction resulting in patient harm, a department implements an emergency verbal double-check requirement before all contrast injections. Which of the following best characterizes this intervention from an RCA perspective?

choices.text: A high-reliability solution that directly addresses the latent conditions identified in the root cause analysis
A completed corrective action that fulfills the requirements of the root cause analysis process
A behavior-shaping constraint that represents the most durable form of process improvement available
A placeholder intervention that may reduce immediate risk but does not address the root cause

questions.explanation: In the setting of a serious adverse event, immediate interventions may be implemented to quickly reduce the risk of recurrence. However, such rapidly generated solutions typically do not address the underlying root cause and should serve only as a placeholder until more reliable and sustainable solutions can be developed, tested, and implemented through the full RCA process. A verbal double-check is a relatively low-reliability solution that depends on consistent human behavior and does not modify the system conditions that contributed to the original event.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which coil produces the static magnetic field (B₀)?

choices.text: Main coil
Gradient coils
RF coils
All coils contribute variably to the static magnetic field

questions.explanation: The static magnetic field (B₀) is generated by the superconducting main coil. The gradient coils produce the time-varying gradient magnetic field (dB/dt) used for spatial localization, and the RF coils generate the time-varying radiofrequency magnetic field (B₁). The main magnetic field is always on and cannot simply be switched off.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: How is the main coil assembly of an MRI scanner cooled?

choices.text: Liquid helium
Chilled water
Liquid nitrogen
Forced air circulation

questions.explanation: The superconducting main coil is contained in a helium-cooled cryogenic assembly, while the gradient and RF transmit coils are contained in a non-cryogenic assembly cooled by chilled water. This distinction is clinically important because the main coil's liquid helium cooling system is directly involved in the physics of a quench. The use of liquid nitrogen (option C) is incorrect.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: To whom do MRI-related risks apply?

choices.text: To patients who have known metallic implants or devices
To MRI technologists who spend extended time in the magnet room
To all who may enter the MRI scanner environment
To all patients undergoing MRI

questions.explanation: MRI-related risks apply to all who may enter the MRI scanner environment, including patients, research subjects, MRI personnel, and visitors. Greater risk exists specifically for non-MR personnel who do not regularly work in the MR environment - such as physicians and nurses who may enter urgently - as well as improperly trained staff such as security and cleaning personnel who may unknowingly bring ferromagnetic materials into the environment. Patients' family members who accompany them can also be overlooked.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following professionals typically fills the role of MR Medical Director (MRMD)?

choices.text: Radiologist
MR technologist
MR physicist
Hospital administrator

questions.explanation: The MRMD is a physician-level role typically filled by a radiologist. The MRMD assumes ultimate responsibility for a site's operational MR safety and the safe execution of all MR examinations.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the primary responsibilities of the MR Medical Director (MRMD)?

choices.text: Ensuring MR safety policies are followed and that emergency procedures are in place
Rendering expertise on safe scanning conditions for patients with implanted devices
Assuming ultimate responsibility for the site's operational MR safety
Personally performing and supervising all MR examinations conducted within the department

questions.explanation: The MRMD is a physician-level role that assumes ultimate responsibility for a site's operational MR safety and the safe execution of all MR examinations. The MRMD appoints MRSOs and MRSEs, maintains MR safety policies and procedures, and appropriately investigates any MR safety adverse events. Option A describes the MRSO. Option B describes the MRSE.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following professionals typically fills the role of MR Safety Officer (MRSO)?

choices.text: Radiologist
MR technologist
MR physicist
Hospital administrator

questions.explanation: The MRSO is a role typically filled by a technologist. Its responsibilities include ensuring that policies and procedures are followed, that emergency procedures are in place and trained for, and that sufficient education is completed by relevant personnel.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the primary responsibilities of the MR Safety Officer (MRSO)?

choices.text: Assuming ultimate responsibility for operational MR safety and investigating adverse events
Ensuring that MR safety policies and procedures are followed
Rendering expertise on safe MR equipment use and providing recommendations for patients with implanted devices
Reviewing all MR safety screening forms and personally approving patients for entry into Zone III

questions.explanation: The MRSO is a role typically filled by a technologist. Its responsibilities include ensuring that policies and procedures are followed, that emergency procedures are in place and trained for, and that sufficient education is completed by relevant personnel, among others. The MRMD (A) holds ultimate responsibility. The MRSE (C) is typically an MR physicist focused on technical expertise.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following professionals typically serves as the MR Safety Expert (MRSE)?

choices.text: Radiologist
MR technologist
MR physicist
Hospital administrator

questions.explanation: The MRSE is typically an MR physicist who serves as a resource for the MRMD and MRSOs, rendering expertise related to the safe use of MR equipment and providing recommendations for appropriate scanning conditions for patients with implanted devices.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the primary responsibilities of the MR Safety Expert (MRSE)?

choices.text: Ensuring day-to-day enforcement of MR safety policies and emergency preparedness
Assuming ultimate responsibility for the safe execution of all MR examinations
Rendering expertise related to the safe use of MR equipment
Coordinating MR safety education and maintaining safety documentation for the department

questions.explanation: The MRSE is typically an MR physicist who serves as a resource for the MRMD and MRSOs. The MRSE renders expertise related to the safe use of MR equipment and provides recommendations for appropriate scanning conditions for patients with implanted devices. This distinguishes the MRSE from the MRSO, who handles operational and educational responsibilities, and from the MRMD, who holds ultimate responsibility and authority.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which MRI zone describes the area freely accessible to the public?

choices.text: Zone I
Zone II
Zone III
Zone IV

questions.explanation: Zone I includes all areas that are freely accessible to the public - this is the area through which patients and others pass before they access the controlled MR environment. It is unrestricted and requires no special supervision or access controls. Zone II is the interface zone where patient screening occurs. Zone III requires strict physical restrictions. Zone IV is the magnet room itself.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which MRI zone describes the waiting area of the MRI facility where patients are greeted and histories are obtained?

choices.text: Zone I
Zone II
Zone III
Zone IV

questions.explanation: Zone II is the interface between the uncontrolled Zone I and the strictly controlled Zones III and IV. It is used to greet patients, obtain patient histories, and screen patients for MR safety issues. Patients in Zone II should be under the supervision of MR personnel. Zone III, which typically houses the scanner control room, requires additional physical access restrictions.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which MRI zone houses the control room?

choices.text: Zone I
Zone II
Zone III
Zone IV

questions.explanation: Zone III is a strictly controlled area near the scanner that requires physical restrictions such as locks or passkey systems, and access only under MR personnel supervision. The scanner control room is typically in Zone III. Zone IV - not Zone III - is the magnet room itself and the highest risk area, containing the Projectile Zone.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient develops cardiac arrest while inside the MRI scanner room (Zone IV). Which of the following best describes the most appropriate initial response?

choices.text: Immediately initiate a quench to eliminate the magnetic field before providing resuscitation
Begin life support procedures in the scanner room itself
Evacuate all personnel from the scanner room and await complete magnetic field dissipation before entering to provide care
Bring the crash cart into the scanner room

questions.explanation: When a medical emergency occurs, MR trained and certified personnel should begin basic life support or CPR in Zone IV if required, while urgently moving the patient from Zone IV to a magnetically safe location to allow others to assist in a safe environment outside the scan room. A quench should not be initiated in this scenario, as the magnetic field itself is not the source of the emergency - it is a medical event unrelated to the magnet. The crash cart should remain outside Zone IV.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best distinguishes MR Level 2 personnel from MR Level 1 personnel?

choices.text: Level 2 personnel may work independently in Zone IV; Level 1 personnel require physician supervision
Level 1 personnel cannot be independently responsible for the safety of others in Zone IV
Level 1 personnel are restricted to Zone III
Level 1 are technologists only; Level 2 are physicians and physicists only

questions.explanation: Level 1 personnel have passed the facility's basic MR safety education requirements to ensure they would not be a danger to themselves or others, but are not independently responsible for the safety of others in Zone IV. Level 2 personnel are more extensively trained - including on topics such as RF-induced heating - and can be independently responsible for the safety of others in Zone IV. Importantly, a technologist should not work alone; there should always be at least one Level 2 technologist assisted by an additional MR-trained individual present in Zone III.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best defines an "MR Safe" item?

choices.text: An item that can be safely used in the MRI environment under specific conditions
An item that is nonhazardous in all MRI environments
Any metal-containing item that has been tested and shown to produce minimal deflection forces at field strengths up to 3 Tesla
Any item approved for use in Zone III by a licensed independent practitioner following a risk-benefit assessment

questions.explanation: An MR Safe item contains no metal and is composed of materials that are nonconductive, nonmetallic, and nonmagnetic - making it nonhazardous in all MRI environments. A plastic tube is the prototypical example. Option A describes MR Conditional. Option C is incorrect because metal-containing items can never be classified as MR Safe regardless of deflection testing results.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following items would be classified as MR Unsafe?

choices.text: A titanium aneurysm clip
A nitinol vascular stent
A plastic drainage tube
A ferromagnetic aneurysm clip

questions.explanation: MR Unsafe items are contraindicated and must be kept outside the MR scanner room. A ferromagnetic aneurysm clip is the prototypical example of an MR Unsafe device. A titanium aneurysm clip (A) and a nitinol stent (B) are examples of MR Conditional devices. A plastic tube (C) is MR Safe. The distinction between ferromagnetic and non-ferromagnetic metals is critical to this classification.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT typically among the conditions that must be verified before scanning a patient with an MR Conditional implanted device?

choices.text: Magnetic field strength
Scanner model year and gradient coil manufacturer
Defined SAR or RF deposition limits
Specific permissible RF coils

questions.explanation: MR Conditional labeling specifies the exact conditions under which a device has been demonstrated safe, which typically include the magnetic field strength, the specific RF coils permitted for use, and defined RF deposition parameters such as a SAR limit. Scanner model year and gradient coil manufacturer are not standard conditional parameters and are not required for safe scanning decisions. Failing to verify any of the true conditional parameters before scanning could expose the patient to significant harm.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient is found to have a titanium surgical clip placed during a prior cholecystectomy. Which of the following most accurately describes the MR safety classification of this implant?

choices.text: Titanium clips may be considered MR Safe because titanium is a non-ferromagnetic material
Metal-containing implants can never be considered MR Safe
The clip can be assumed to be MR Safe if the patient has undergone prior MRI examinations without reported complications
The classification depends on whether the clip produces susceptibility artifact on prior imaging

questions.explanation: All metal-containing implants are considered either MR Unsafe or MR Conditional - they are never classified as MR Safe. Even non-ferromagnetic metals such as titanium can be subject to translational and rotational forces, and conducting metals can generate current from RF and gradient field interactions. Therefore, a titanium clip would be MR Conditional rather than MR Safe. The absence of prior complications (C) is insufficient to determine MR safety classification.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the role of ferromagnetic detection devices in MR safety screening?

choices.text: They replace the need for screening questionnaires
They augment safety screening by helping to identify unknown ferromagnetic objects
They are used exclusively to screen non-patient personnel entering Zone IV for concealed ferromagnetic objects
They are the primary method for determining whether a specific implant is MR Safe, Conditional, or Unsafe

questions.explanation: Ferromagnetic detection devices - either wall-mounted or handheld - augment safety screening processes by helping to identify unknown ferromagnetic objects concealed on a patient, and can detect some superficial internal implants such as pacemakers. All MR sites should have a handheld magnet of at least 1000 Gauss for these purposes. They supplement but do not replace formal screening processes, and cannot definitively determine MR safety classification of implanted devices.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A technologist carrying a ferromagnetic instrument while walking toward the MRI scanner notices only minimal magnetic pull. A few steps closer, the instrument is suddenly and forcefully ripped from her hand. Which of the following best explains this phenomenon?

choices.text: The magnetic field increases linearly with proximity to the magnet, generating sudden maximum force at the scanner's edge
The spatial gradient magnetic field increases steeply in close proximity to the magnet
The instrument became magnetized as it approached the scanner, exponentially increasing its ferromagnetic susceptibility
The floor of Zone IV amplifies the magnetic field at ground level, creating unexpectedly high forces for objects carried at waist height

questions.explanation: Magnetic attraction does NOT increase linearly as one approaches the magnet. Rather, the spatial gradient magnetic field increases very steeply in close proximity to the scanner. As a result, one can perceive very little magnetic pull on a ferromagnetic object at a distance, and then when moving only a small distance closer, the object is subjected to a tremendously higher attractive force - typically ripping it from one's grasp. This is why the ACR Manual on MR Safety now recommends pocketless attire for MR personnel who work in Zone IV on a daily basis.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient is brought emergently for MRI and is unable to provide a history. Which of the following best describes the appropriate approach to MR safety screening?

choices.text: MRI should be deferred until the patient regains capacity to provide a complete history
History should be obtained from available sources before deciding whether to proceed
A signed waiver from the referring physician is sufficient to proceed
The patient may enter Zone IV if no external ferromagnetic objects are visibly identified

questions.explanation: When screening is more difficult because the patient is unconscious or otherwise unable to provide a reliable history, screening information should be obtained as best as possible from other sources, including family members, the medical record, and available prior imaging. A physical examination by trained MR personnel should be performed to assess for surgical scars. The urgency of the examination should be balanced with the level of uncertainty in the screening process.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient has a documented history of an eye injury from a metallic foreign body, and there is uncertainty as to whether retained intraocular metal may be present. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step before proceeding with MRI?

choices.text: Ultrasound of the orbits to assess for intraocular foreign body
Orbital X-rays or thin-section head CT to assess for retained intraocular metal
Low field strength MRI of the orbits as a preliminary screening examination
No additional imaging is necessary if the patient denies current visual symptoms

questions.explanation: When there is a documented history of eye injury from metal and uncertainty as to whether there may be retained intraocular metal, imaging is recommended prior to MRI - which may include either orbital X-rays or thin-section head CT. Ultrasound (A) is not the recommended modality for this indication. Low-field MRI (C) would itself pose a risk to a patient with retained intraocular metal. The absence of symptoms (D) does not exclude retained metal. 9 GAUSS LINE

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: What field strength is present at the required safety demarcation line based on most recently revised guidelines?

choices.text: 0.5 mT
0.9 mT
5.0 mT
9.0 mT

questions.explanation: 9 Gauss is equivalent to 0.9 mT (1 Tesla = 10,000 Gauss; therefore 9 Gauss = 0.0009 Tesla = 0.9 mT). This line should be marked on the floors and walls for safety, and because the magnetic field is three-dimensional, the restricted area may extend through the floor and/or ceiling to adjacent floors. The change from 5 Gauss (0.5 mT) to 9 Gauss (0.9 mT) was recognized by the FDA and endorsed by the ACR MR Safety Committee in 2024.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: The IEC recently changed the required safety demarcation line for cardiac implantable electronic devices from the 5 Gauss line to the 9 Gauss line. Which of the following correctly describes the spatial relationship between these two lines and their implication for site compliance?

choices.text: Sites using the 5 Gauss standard are required to expand their restricted area outward
Sites using the 5 Gauss standard are already compliant with the new 9 Gauss requirement
The two lines are at the same distance from the magnet but represent different international measurement conventions
Sites using the 5 Gauss standard have the option to expand their restricted area outward for enhanced security

questions.explanation: Because the 9 Gauss line is closer to the magnet than the 5 Gauss line (9 Gauss is a higher field strength and occurs nearer the source), the 9 Gauss line falls within the boundary defined by the 5 Gauss line. Sites that have been following 5 Gauss recommendations - maintaining restricted access beyond the more conservative 5 Gauss boundary - are therefore already compliant with the less restrictive 9 Gauss standard. The revision still allows for a 1 Gauss tolerance for variability in device testing methods, since CIED manufacturers have been required to demonstrate device immunity to static magnetic fields up to 10 Gauss.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient with a known intracranial aneurysm clip requires MRI. The family reports that the patient underwent MRI at an outside hospital two years ago without apparent complications. The specific manufacturer and model of the clip cannot be identified. Which of the following best describes the appropriate course of action?

choices.text: Proceed with MRI at any field strength
Proceed with MRI at 1.5T or below
MRI should not be performed until further device information is obtained
Proceed with MRI as long as emergency personnel are on standby

questions.explanation: There has been at least one documented fatality due to rotation of an MR Unsafe ferromagnetic aneurysm clip while the patient was in the MRI scanner. If a patient is identified to have an intracranial aneurysm clip, MRI should not be performed until the specific manufacturer, model, and type of each clip is definitively identified and its MR safety conditions are established. Although a patient may previously have undergone MRI with an aneurysm clip without known complications, that fact alone is explicitly stated to be insufficient to conclude that the clip is MR Conditional.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs) can be adversely affected by the magnetic fields of an MRI scanner. Which of the following is NOT listed as a potential MRI-related complication in patients with CIEDs?

choices.text: Failure to pace
Induction of ventricular fibrillation
Heating of cardiac tissue adjacent to the leads
Complete demagnetization of the implanted pulse generator

questions.explanation: The listed MRI-related complications of CIEDs include failure to pace, induction of ventricular fibrillation, and heating of cardiac tissue adjacent to the leads - all of which can potentially be fatal. CIEDs can be adversely affected by the B₀, B₁, and dB/dt fields. Complete demagnetization of the pulse generator is not among the listed complications.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: MRI is planned for a patient with a pacemaker that carries an MR Conditional label. Which of the following best describes the required approach?

choices.text: Only field strength must be verified; other parameters are left to the radiologist's discretion
All conditions must be followed in their entirety for every single exam
Conditions apply to the initial examination only; subsequent studies may proceed without re-verification
Conditions apply only to the pulse generator; the leads do not require independent verification

questions.explanation: If MRI is performed on a patient with an MR Conditional CIED, the conditions for scanning must be followed in their entirety. This includes attention to magnet field strength, scanning parameters, and cardiology programming of the device, as well as monitoring throughout the exam in the presence of ACLS-trained personnel with a crash cart available should resuscitation be necessary. Selective adherence to only some conditions (A) is insufficient. Precise identification of each component of the device system - including both the pulse generator and the leads - is essential.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Regarding CIED systems that are NOT specifically labeled as MR Conditional, which of the following statements is most accurate?

choices.text: Absolutely contraindicated
May be scanned at some centers if specific institutional and patient-level requirements are met
Permitted at any institution with written informed consent
Permitted only at academic medical centers with dedicated cardiac electrophysiology programs on site

questions.explanation: CIED systems not specifically labeled as MR Conditional are being scanned at some centers in an informed consent manner following guidelines established by the Heart Rhythm Society and the ACR. This requires a specific set of institutional and patient-level elements to be in place. The blanket classification of these devices as MR Unsafe (A) does not reflect current practice guidelines.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as a required element for scanning a CIED not specifically labeled as MR Conditional?

choices.text: An institutional protocol in place with a responsible MRMD and CIED physician using a radiology/cardiology team approach
Medical necessity must be established for the MRI examination
The patient must be observed for a minimum of 24 hours following the MRI examination
Appropriate CIED reprogramming must occur after the MRI

questions.explanation: The six required elements for scanning a non-labeled CIED are: (1) an institutional protocol with a responsible MRMD and CIED physician using a team approach, (2) established medical necessity for the exam, (3) patient monitoring including ECG and pulse oximetry during the exam, (4) a defibrillator/monitor with external pacing available outside Zone IV, (5) ACLS personnel in attendance during the exam, and (6) appropriate CIED reprogramming post-MRI. A mandatory 24-hour post-MRI observation period is not among the listed requirements.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the current evidence and recommendations regarding MRI exposure without gadolinium-based contrast in pregnant patients?

choices.text: MRI is absolutely contraindicated in the first trimester due to teratogenic effects of radiofrequency fields on organogenesis
Noncontrast MRI up to 3T has not been shown to harm the developing fetus
MRI is safe during pregnancy only at 1.5T or below, regardless of trimester
MRI requires documented authorization from a maternal-fetal medicine specialist

questions.explanation: MRI exposure alone, without the administration of gadolinium-based contrast media, has not been shown to have a detrimental effect on the developing fetus. For this reason, no special consideration is recommended during pregnancy for noncontrast MRI up to 3T at normal operating mode. However, since it is impossible to completely eliminate all risk, patients and clinicians should consider whether it is safe to delay an MRI examination until the end of pregnancy.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A radiology technologist who is 20 weeks pregnant works in an MRI department. Which of the following best describes the applicable MR safety recommendations for her?

choices.text: She must be placed on modified duty and may not enter any MRI zone beyond Zone II for the duration of her pregnancy
She may work in the MRI environment during all stages of pregnancy but should not remain in Zone IV during data acquisition or scanning
She may work without restriction in all MRI zones throughout her entire pregnancy
She must obtain written clearance from her obstetrician before working in Zone III or Zone IV

questions.explanation: Pregnant healthcare workers may work in the MRI environment during all stages of pregnancy. However, they should not remain in Zone IV during data acquisition or scanning. This precaution is distinct from the recommendations for pregnant patients, for whom the evidence supports the safety of noncontrast MRI up to 3T.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: The possibility of thermal injury and burns during MRI is predominantly due to which of the following?

choices.text: Static magnetic field (B₀)
Time-varying gradient magnetic field (dB/dt)
Radiofrequency (RF) fields
Acoustic vibrations from gradient coil switching

questions.explanation: The possibility of thermal injury and burns during MRI is predominantly due to the radiofrequency (RF) fields. The RF coil is the closest to the patient in the magnet bore and poses specific risks. RF fields can induce burns through direct proximity to the scanner bore, through closed-loop current induction, and through heating of conducting materials such as wires, metallic patches, and tattoo pigments.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: During positioning of a large patient for MRI, a technologist considers using a folded hospital sheet in place of a commercial insulating pad to create space between the patient's skin and the inner surface of the scanner bore. Which of the following best describes the appropriateness of this practice?

choices.text: Not recommended
Recommended against
Acceptable if commercial pads are insufficient
Acceptable if the sheet contains no metallic fibers

questions.explanation: Insulating pads are necessary to keep skin at least 1 to 2 centimeters from the scanner surface. Tightly wedging a sheet in place of a pad between the skin and the bore does not maintain the requisite distance and creates a distinct risk of burns. This practice is specifically recommended against in the ACR Manual on MR Safety. Commercial pads with strategically placed notches are available for patients in whom standard positioning creates skin-to-skin or skin-to-bore contact risks.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: During patient positioning for MRI, a technologist observes that the patient's inner thighs are in contact with each other. Which of the following best explains the potential burn hazard associated with this finding?

choices.text: Friction between adjacent skin surfaces
Formation of a closed loop
Adjacent skin surfaces reflect RF energy back toward the RF coil
Skin-to-skin contact traps heat generated by gradient coil switching

questions.explanation: RF fields can induce currents within the body when a closed loop is formed - for example, when there is skin-to-skin contact at the inner thighs. When the contact surface area is small, the current density becomes concentrated, and resistive heating can lead to burns. Skin-to-skin contact burns have also occurred when a finger contacts the thigh, or when an overhanging abdominal panniculus contacts the upper thigh in obese patients. Commercial pads with strategically placed notches to keep the thighs separated are available to minimize this risk.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why leads and conductors from physiologic monitoring equipment pose an unpredictable burn risk that may vary between different MRI scanners?

choices.text: Leads act as antennae that absorb static magnetic field energy and convert it directly to thermal energy
Leads from monitoring equipment contain ferromagnetic alloys that become heated by the gradient magnetic field through eddy current induction
The RF resonant wavelength is a function of magnet field strength, causing leads and conductors to have unpredictable heating tendencies in different magnets
Physiologic monitoring leads emit competing radiofrequency signals that interfere with scanner calibration and generate heat in adjacent tissues

questions.explanation: Since the RF resonant wavelength is a function of magnet field strength, leads and other conductors can have drastically different and unpredictable tendencies to heat in different magnets. Care must be taken to prevent wire loops or metallic patches from touching patients' skin during routine scanning. This unpredictability means that a configuration that is safe at one field strength may be hazardous at another.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient with a large decorative tattoo on the lower back is being prepared for a lumbar spine MRI. Which of the following is the most accurate statement regarding this patient's burn risk?

choices.text: Tattoos contain no metallic compounds and pose no burn risk during MRI
Tattoos may occasionally undergo RF-induced heating and cause burns
The patient must be scanned at 1.5T or below to eliminate the burn risk from tattoo pigments
Tattoos are classified as MR Conditional and require documentation of pigment composition before scanning

questions.explanation: Large tattoos may occasionally undergo heating during MRI and cause burns. When tattoo-related burn risk is a concern, application of a cold compress or ice pack may be necessary to reduce the risk of skin burning. There is no categorical field strength limit specifically associated with tattoo-related burns; the risk varies with tattoo size, composition, and location relative to the RF field.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient scheduled for MRI is wearing a foil-backed transdermal clonidine patch. The patch is removed before scanning. Which of the following is the most important safety consideration associated with this removal?

choices.text: The removed patch must be stored in a shielded container outside Zone IV
Medication replacement must be ensured after the MRI
A sterile dressing must be applied to the patch site before the patient enters the scanner room
The patch manufacturer must be contacted to verify the residual medication is safe during MRI

questions.explanation: Foil-backed transdermal medication patches can be rapidly heated by RF pulses during MRI and must be removed before scanning. However, when patches are removed, there must be a clear line of communication to ensure medication replacement after the MRI - particularly for critical medications such as clonidine foil-backed patches, where abrupt discontinuation can have significant clinical consequences. Medication continuity is the most clinically important consideration following patch removal.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A staff member is found pinned against the MRI scanner by a ferromagnetic hospital gurney and cannot be freed by manual effort. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?

choices.text: Attempt to free the staff member using additional personnel leverage while awaiting the MRSO
Initiate a quench to eliminate the magnetic field
Evacuate all other personnel from Zone IV and await spontaneous resolution of the magnetic force
Move the patient currently on the scanner table out of Zone IV first before addressing the pinned staff member

questions.explanation: A quench is indicated when the presence of the magnetic field poses an immediate risk to human life or health - the prototypical example being when personnel are pinned to the magnet by a ferromagnetic object such as a hospital gurney. Unlike most medical equipment, an MRI magnet cannot simply be switched on and off; initiating a quench is the only way to rapidly eliminate the magnetic field. The decision to quench should not be taken lightly given the significant consequences, but this scenario represents the clearest indication.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient in the MRI scanner room develops ventricular fibrillation during an examination. No ferromagnetic object is entrapping the patient or any personnel. Which of the following best describes the appropriate management approach?

choices.text: Immediately initiate a quench to allow full ACLS access and use of defibrillation equipment in Zone IV
Begin CPR in Zone IV
Initiate a quench and administer ACLS medications simultaneously to maximize efficiency
Evacuate all personnel from Zone IV and initiate a quench before re-entering to provide resuscitation

questions.explanation: A quench is reserved specifically for situations in which the magnetic field itself poses an immediate risk to life or health. Cardiac arrest is a medical emergency unrelated to the magnetic field, and initiating a quench in this scenario would cause significant collateral harm without addressing the actual emergency. The correct response is to begin CPR in Zone IV if immediately needed while urgently moving the patient to a magnetically safe location outside Zone IV, where a full resuscitation team with appropriate equipment can assist.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: During a quench, liquid helium rapidly boils into gas and expands dramatically. If the quench pipe fails or becomes obstructed, what is the most immediate risk?

choices.text: Projectile injury
Asphyxiation
Electrical fire
Hypothermia

questions.explanation: When the quench pipe fails or is obstructed during a quench, rapidly expanding helium gas is released directly into Zone IV. Because helium is lighter than air, it rapidly displaces oxygen throughout the room - particularly near the floor - creating an immediate risk of hypoxia and asphyxiation. The liquid helium also boils off as an extremely cold gas, producing dense condensation fog that severely reduces visibility and complicates safe egress. For these reasons, emergency procedures for a quench must always include immediate evacuation of Zone IV. The liquid helium involved in sustaining the main magnetic field typically occupies 1,500 to 2,000 liters and expands by a factor of approximately 760 when it vaporizes.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Many contemporary MRI installations incorporate pressure-equalization mechanisms in the magnet room. This design feature is primarily intended to mitigate which of the following hazards?

choices.text: Negative pressure that draws ferromagnetic objects into the magnet room
Positive-pressure entrapment during a quench
Pressure fluctuations from gradient coil switching
Differential pressure that prevents the quench pipe from venting helium gas to the external atmosphere

questions.explanation: Inward-swinging doors in the magnet room may create a risk of positive-pressure entrapment during rapid gas expansion in a quench - the expanding helium gas could exert sufficient pressure against inward-swinging doors to prevent them from being opened, trapping personnel inside Zone IV. Most contemporary MRI installations incorporate pressure-equalization mechanisms designed to mitigate this hazard by preventing differential pressure buildup across the door.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Lipiodol is unique among iodinated contrast media in which of the following ways?

choices.text: It is the only nonionic dimeric agent
It is the only currently approved water-insoluble iodinated contrast medium
It is the only iso-osmolar iodinated contrast agent
It is the only agent approved for intrathecal use

questions.explanation: Lipiodol is the only currently approved water-insoluble iodinated contrast medium. All other iodinated contrast media are water-soluble. Water-soluble agents are derived from tri-iodinated benzene rings and are classified as ionic or nonionic, and monomeric or dimeric.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: At standard iodine concentrations, ionic monomeric contrast media have approximately what osmolality relative to human serum?

choices.text: Equal to serum (iso-osmolar)
Roughly twice that of serum
Roughly four times that of serum
Roughly eight times that of serum

questions.explanation: At standard iodine concentrations, ionic monomeric contrast media have the highest osmolality of all iodinated contrast agents - roughly four times that of human serum. They are therefore referred to as high-osmolality contrast media. Nonionic monomers have roughly twice the osmolality of serum (low-osmolality), and nonionic dimers have osmolality similar to plasma (iso-osmolality).

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the osmolality of nonionic monomeric contrast media relative to human serum?

choices.text: Iso-osmolar
Roughly twice that of serum
Roughly four times that of serum
Roughly half that of serum

questions.explanation: Nonionic monomeric contrast media have about half the osmolality of ionic monomers - roughly twice that of human serum. This is why they are referred to as low-osmolality contrast media. Nonionic dimers have osmolality similar to plasma and are referred to as iso-osmolality contrast media.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following is an approved indication for intravenous injection of ionic monomeric contrast media in the United States?

choices.text: CT of the abdomen and pelvis
CT pulmonary angiography
Intravenous urography
None of the above

questions.explanation: Ionic monomeric contrast media have roughly four times the osmolality of human serum and are associated with higher rates of adverse reactions than nonionic agents. For this reason, they are not employed routinely for intravenous injection in the United States. They may be used for intra-arterial injection in certain settings.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following is the only iso-osmolar contrast agent currently approved for intravenous use?

choices.text: Iohexol (Omnipaque®)
Iopamidol (Isovue®)
Iodixanol (Visipaque®)
Ioversol (Optiray®)

questions.explanation: Iodixanol (Visipaque®) is the only iso-osmolar contrast agent approved for IV use. It is a nonionic dimer with osmolality similar to that of plasma. The other agents listed - iohexol, iopamidol, and ioversol - are nonionic monomers with low osmolality (roughly twice that of serum). Iso-osmolality media are sometimes preferred for intra-arterial injection as they cause less discomfort than nonionic monomers when injected into arteries.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Adverse contrast reactions of any type have been reported in up to what percentage of patients injected with nonionic contrast material?

choices.text: Less than 1%
Up to 3%
Up to 10%
Up to 15%

questions.explanation: Adverse contrast reactions of any type have been reported in up to 3% of patients injected with nonionic contrast material, though some series have reported a much lower frequency. Allergic-like reactions are encountered in less than 1% of patients. Severe life-threatening allergic-like reactions are extremely rare, estimated at 0.01% to 0.04% of injected patients. PHYSIOLOGIC VS. ALLERGIC-LIKE REACTIONS

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of physiologic contrast reactions?

choices.text: IgE-mediated hypersensitivity to iodine
Direct, dose-dependent toxic effects of the contrast medium
Antigen-antibody complex deposition in small vessels
T-cell mediated delayed hypersensitivity

questions.explanation: Physiologic reactions are dose related and represent direct toxic effects of the injected contrast medium. They are less likely to occur, and less likely to be severe, when lower doses are administered. Unlike allergic-like reactions, they do not require prior sensitization.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why contrast reactions are classified as "allergic-like" rather than truly "allergic" in most patients?

choices.text: They occur only after repeated exposures
Prior sensitization is not required
They are mediated exclusively by complement activation
They occur only with ionic contrast agents

questions.explanation: The mechanism of allergic-like reactions is not understood in most patients. In most cases, these reactions do not represent the antigen-IgE antibody response characteristic of true allergic reactions such as those to penicillin. Because prior sensitization is not required, these reactions are considered "allergic-like" rather than truly "allergic." They are idiosyncratic and can occur from any administered volume of contrast media.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient develops nausea, vomiting, flushing, warmth, and a spontaneously resolving vasovagal reaction shortly after IV contrast administration. How should these findings be classified?

choices.text: Mild allergic-like reaction
Mild physiologic reaction
Moderate physiologic reaction
Moderate allergic-like reaction

questions.explanation: Mild physiologic reactions include nausea, vomiting, flushing, warmth, chills, headache, anxiety, altered taste, mild hypertension, and spontaneously resolving vasovagal reactions. These are self-limited and resolve without progression. Mild allergic-like reactions, by contrast, include hives, pruritus, limited cutaneous edema, and nasal symptoms.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a mild allergic-like reaction to iodinated contrast?

choices.text: Nausea and vomiting
Protracted nausea with chest pain
Hives and pruritus
Diffuse erythema with stable vital signs

questions.explanation: Mild allergic-like reactions include few hives, pruritus, limited cutaneous edema, itchy/scratchy throat, nasal congestion, repetitive sneezing, and stuffy nose - all self-limited and resolving without progression. Nausea and vomiting are mild physiologic reactions. Protracted nausea with chest pain is a moderate physiologic reaction. Diffuse erythema with stable vital signs is a moderate allergic-like reaction.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a moderate physiologic reaction to iodinated contrast?

choices.text: Spontaneously resolving vasovagal reaction
Vasovagal reaction responsive to treatment
Vasovagal reaction resistant to treatment
Few hives with pruritus

questions.explanation: Moderate reactions are more pronounced and commonly require medical management. Moderate physiologic reactions include protracted nausea, chest pain, and a vasovagal reaction that requires and is responsive to treatment. A spontaneously resolving vasovagal reaction is a mild physiologic reaction. A vasovagal reaction resistant to treatment is a severe physiologic reaction.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient receiving iodinated contrast develops diffuse hives, diffuse erythema with stable vital signs, and facial edema without dyspnea. Which category best describes this reaction?

choices.text: Mild allergic-like
Moderate allergic-like
Severe allergic-like
Moderate physiologic

questions.explanation: Moderate allergic-like reactions include diffuse hives, diffuse erythema with stable vital signs, facial edema without dyspnea, and wheezing with mild or no hypoxia. These are more pronounced than mild reactions and commonly require medical management. Severe allergic-like reactions involve dyspnea, hypotension, laryngeal edema, or significant hypoxia.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following is classified as a severe physiologic reaction to iodinated contrast?

choices.text: Diffuse facial edema with dyspnea
Laryngeal edema with stridor
Arrhythmia
Diffuse erythema with stable vital signs

questions.explanation: Severe physiologic reactions are potentially life-threatening and include vasovagal reaction resistant to treatment, arrhythmia, seizures, hypertensive crisis, pulmonary edema, and cardiopulmonary arrest. Diffuse facial edema with dyspnea and laryngeal edema with stridor are severe allergic-like reactions. Diffuse erythema with stable vital signs is a moderate allergic-like reaction.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Pulmonary edema and cardiopulmonary arrest can be symptoms of which of the following?

choices.text: Moderate physiologic reaction
Severe physiologic reaction
Severe allergic-like reaction
Either severe physiologic or severe allergic-like reactions

questions.explanation: Pulmonary edema and cardiopulmonary arrest can be symptoms of either severe physiologic reactions or severe allergic-like reactions. This overlap underscores why the clinical distinction between physiologic and allergic-like reactions can be difficult in severe presentations.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Compared to the general population, a patient with a prior allergic-like reaction to iodinated contrast has approximately what increased risk of another reaction to the same class of contrast?

choices.text: 2x
5x

questions.explanation: Patients with a history of a prior allergic-like reaction to the same class of contrast media are believed to have approximately five times the risk of the general population for another allergic-like reaction. Patients with other allergies or asthma are about two to three times as likely to react - a meaningfully lower risk than those with a prior contrast-specific reaction.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT considered an independent risk factor for an allergic-like reaction to iodinated contrast media beyond that of general allergies?

choices.text: Prior allergic-like reaction to iodinated contrast
Asthma
Shellfish allergy
Multiple other allergies

questions.explanation: Allergies to shellfish or other iodine-containing products such as povidone-iodine (Betadine®) are not believed to increase the risk of an allergic-like contrast reaction beyond that of other general allergies. The highest-risk patients are those with a prior allergic-like reaction to the same class of contrast media; asthma and multiple allergies confer a two to three times elevated risk.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient with a prior allergic-like reaction to a gadolinium-based contrast agent (GBCM) is about to receive iodinated contrast. How does this history affect the risk of an allergic-like reaction?

choices.text: Increases risk approximately five times above the general population
Increases risk approximately two to three times above the general population
Does not increase risk above that of other general allergies
Confers no increased risk of reaction to iodinated contrast whatsoever

questions.explanation: A history of a prior allergic-like reaction to gadolinium-based contrast media is not believed to increase the risk of an allergic-like reaction to iodinated contrast agents above that of other allergies - and vice versa. The significantly elevated risk (approximately five times the general population) applies specifically to a prior reaction to the same class of contrast media as that being administered.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following underlying conditions may be exacerbated by administration of iodinated contrast media?

choices.text: Cardiac arrhythmias, myasthenia gravis, and severe hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism
Diabetes mellitus and hypothyroidism
Hypertension, asthma, and multiple myeloma
Renal artery stenosis and pheochromocytoma

questions.explanation: Underlying diseases that may be exacerbated by contrast media - classified as non-allergic-like reactions - include severe chronic kidney disease or AKI, cardiac arrhythmias, congestive heart failure, myasthenia gravis, and severe hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism. These are distinct from allergic-like reactions and represent direct disease-specific risks.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient with hyperthyroidism is scheduled for radioactive iodine therapy. They have recently received IV iodinated contrast. What washout period is suggested before proceeding?

choices.text: 3-4 weeks
1-2 weeks
6 weeks
3 months

questions.explanation: Iodinated contrast medium can interfere with uptake of both therapeutic and diagnostic radioactive iodine doses. A washout period of 3-4 weeks is suggested for patients with hyperthyroidism before radioactive iodine administration. For patients with hypothyroidism, a longer washout period of 6 weeks is suggested.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient with hypothyroidism requires radioactive iodine imaging of the thyroid and has recently received IV iodinated contrast. What washout period is suggested before proceeding?

choices.text: 2 weeks
3-4 weeks
6 weeks
8-12 weeks

questions.explanation: For patients with hypothyroidism, a washout period of 6 weeks is suggested before radioactive iodine therapy or imaging - longer than the 3-4 weeks recommended for patients with hyperthyroidism. Iodinated contrast medium can interfere with the uptake of the treatment or diagnostic dose of radioactive iodine.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: According to the ACR Manual on Contrast Media (2024), premedication is suggested for which of the following patients?

choices.text: All patients with any prior allergic reaction of any kind
Patients with asthma or multiple drug allergies
Patients with a prior allergic-like to the same class of contrast media
Patients with a prior allergic-like reaction to any class of contrast media

questions.explanation: The ACR Manual on Contrast Media (2024) suggests premedication only for patients who have had a prior allergic-like or unknown-type reaction to the same class of contrast media as that to be administered. The ACR does NOT recommend routine premedication for patients with other allergies, asthma, or prior reactions to a different class of contrast media (e.g., iodinated contrast in a patient with a prior GBCM reaction).

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: What is the only proven benefit of corticosteroid premedication before contrast administration?

choices.text: Reduction in moderate reactions
Reduction in severe and life-threatening reactions
Reduction in mild reactions
Elimination of breakthrough reactions

questions.explanation: The only proven benefit of corticosteroid premedication is a reduction in the number of mild reactions. Studies demonstrating this reduction did not include sufficient numbers of patients with moderate, severe, or life-threatening reactions to draw statistically significant conclusions about premedication's effect on those reactions. It is generally assumed that premedication has a positive effect on severe reactions, but this has not been definitively proven.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes accepted adult premedication regimens before contrast administration?

choices.text: Prednisone 50 mg at 13, 7, and 1 hours before injection; diphenhydramine 50 mg 1 hour before
Methylprednisolone 32 mg at 12 and 2 hours before injection
Both A and B are accepted adult regimens
Prednisone 50 mg once 12 hours before injection; no antihistamine required

questions.explanation: Two common adult premedication regimens are described. The first involves oral prednisone 50 mg at 13, 7, and 1 hours before injection, plus oral diphenhydramine 50 mg 1 hour before injection. The second involves oral methylprednisolone 32 mg at 12 and 2 hours before contrast injection. Both are accepted. A 1- or 2-hour oral regimen has been proven ineffective.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following oral premedication timing approaches has been proven ineffective?

choices.text: 13-hour regimen
12-hour regimen
1- to 2-hour regimen
Rapid IV hydrocortisone regimen

questions.explanation: A 1- or 2-hour oral premedication regimen has been proven to be ineffective. The 12- to 13-hour oral regimens are established as effective. The precise minimum effective premedication time is not known, but the available evidence supports the longer preparation windows.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A child with a prior allergic-like contrast reaction requires premedication. Which of the following correctly describes the recommended pediatric regimen?
