choices.text: Prednisone 0.5-0.7 mg/kg at 13, 7, and 1 hours; diphenhydramine 1 mg/kg 1 hour before
Prednisone 50 mg flat dose at 13, 7, and 1 hours; diphenhydramine 25 mg flat dose 1 hour before
IV methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg once, 1 hour before injection
No premedication is recommended for children under age 12

questions.explanation: The recommended pediatric premedication regimen involves oral prednisone 0.5-0.7 mg/kg at 13, 7, and 1 hours prior to injection (maximum 50 mg per dose), plus oral diphenhydramine at 1 mg/kg (maximum 50 mg) given 1 hour prior to injection. Weight-based dosing distinguishes the pediatric regimen from the flat adult doses.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes a rapid premedication ("rapid prep") protocol?

choices.text: IV hydrocortisone 200 mg every 4 hours until the study; diphenhydramine 50 mg 1 hour before
Oral methylprednisolone 32 mg 2 hours before injection; no antihistamine
Oral prednisone 50 mg 1 hour before injection; diphenhydramine 50 mg simultaneously
IV dexamethasone 10 mg once; no antihistamine required

questions.explanation: One commonly used rapid prep involves IV hydrocortisone 200 mg every 4 hours until the study is performed - preferably deferring imaging until at least two doses have been given if safe and feasible - plus oral diphenhydramine 50 mg 1 hour before injection. Rapid preps are used when the standard 12-hour oral prep would jeopardize patient health. In true emergencies, contrast may need to be administered without any premedication.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A high-risk patient receives appropriate premedication but still develops an allergic-like contrast reaction. This is best described as which of the following?

choices.text: A breakthrough reaction
An anaphylactic reaction
A premedication failure requiring permanent contrast avoidance
A physiologic reaction unrelated to the prior history

questions.explanation: A contrast reaction that occurs despite premedication is called a breakthrough reaction. Premedication reduces but does not eliminate the risk of contrast reactions. Breakthrough reactions occur in a small number of high-risk patients even with appropriate use of an accepted regimen.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the expected severity of a breakthrough contrast reaction relative to a patient's prior reaction?

choices.text: Usually more severe than the prior reaction
Usually less severe than the prior reaction
Usually of similar severity compared to the prior reaction
No predictable relationship to the prior reaction

questions.explanation: When breakthrough reactions occur, they are of similar severity to the initial reaction approximately 80% of the time, less severe approximately 10% of the time, and more severe approximately 10% of the time. If reinjection is required in the future after a breakthrough reaction, any subsequent breakthrough reaction will most likely be of the same severity as the previous breakthrough. CA-AKI VS. CI-AKI

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best distinguishes contrast-associated AKI (CA-AKI) from contrast-induced AKI (CI-AKI)?

choices.text: CA-AKI is correlative; CI-AKI is a proven subset of CA-AKI
CA-AKI occurs after intra-arterial contrast; CI-AKI occurs after IV contrast
CA-AKI is reversible; CI-AKI results in permanent dysfunction
CA-AKI occurs in patients with normal renal function; CI-AKI requires pre-existing CKD

questions.explanation: CA-AKI is a general term for renal function deterioration occurring after IV contrast; it is a correlative diagnosis - contrast is associated with but not proven to have caused the AKI. CI-AKI is a subset of CA-AKI in which contrast is proven or known to be the cause. Most CA-AKI is not due to CI-AKI. Historically, most published studies incorrectly classified all CA-AKI as CI-AKI, leading to substantially inflated estimates of CI-AKI rates.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: In which of the following patients is true CI-AKI most likely to develop after IV iodinated contrast?

choices.text: eGFR 60 mL/min/1.73 m²
eGFR 45 mL/min/1.73 m²
eGFR 35 mL/min/1.73 m²
eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m²

questions.explanation: CI-AKI is most likely to develop in patients with severe CKD (eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m²) or AKI. In patients with eGFR ≥ 45 mL/min/1.73 m², CI-AKI is very unlikely. In patients with eGFR between 30 and 45, it is questionable. Special precautions for IV contrast are therefore advised only for patients with severe CKD or AKI.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: According to KDIGO criteria, which of the following is NOT a diagnostic criterion of acute kidney injury (AKI)?

choices.text: eGFR decrease >10 mL/min/1.73 m² within 72 hours
≥50% relative creatinine increase
Urine output ≤0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 hour
Absolute creatinine increase ≥0.3 mg/dL

questions.explanation: The Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) organization defines AKI - regardless of cause - as: (1) an absolute serum creatinine increase of at least 0.3 mg/dL; (2) a percentage increase of at least 50% above baseline; or (3) a reduction in urine output to 0.5 mL/kg/h for at least 6 hours. Any one of the three criteria is sufficient.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the typical clinical course of CA-AKI?

choices.text: Creatinine rises within 24 hours, peaks ~day 4, returns to baseline in 7-10 days; oliguria is rare; permanent dysfunction is extremely rare
Creatinine rises immediately, peaks within 24 hours, returns to baseline in 3-4 days; most patients develop oliguria
Most affected patients develop significant oliguria; permanent dysfunction occurs in ~10% of cases
Creatinine rises within 24 hours and rarely returns to baseline; permanent dysfunction affects a substantial minority

questions.explanation: The usual clinical course of CA-AKI (including CI-AKI) involves a rise in serum creatinine beginning within 24 hours of contrast administration, peaking at about 4 days, and usually returning to baseline by 7 to 10 days. Most affected patients do not have oliguria, and it is extremely rare for IV iodinated contrast to cause permanent renal dysfunction.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient with ESRD on chronic hemodialysis, but with residual urine output, requires a contrast-enhanced CT. Which of the following most accurately describes the approach to contrast administration?

choices.text: Contrast is absolutely contraindicated in all ESRD patients on dialysis
Dialysis must occur immediately before contrast injection
Dialysis must occur immediately after contrast injection to remove the agent
The risk of further decrease in urine output is probably only theoretical

questions.explanation: Iodinated contrast media have no significant toxicity if retained in the body, so there is no requirement to time hemodialysis immediately before or after contrast administration. Many nephrologists agree to inject IV contrast in ESRD patients when a contrast-enhanced study is necessary. The risk of further decrease in residual urine output is theoretical, though fluid overload from hyperosmolar contrast media administration is an additional consideration.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Why do some nephrologists advocate more caution when administering iodinated contrast to patients on peritoneal dialysis compared to those on hemodialysis?

choices.text: Peritoneal dialysis is less efficient at removing contrast from the blood
Iodinated contrast is directly toxic to the peritoneal membrane
Residual urine output may be more important to the well-being of peritoneal dialysis patients
Peritoneal dialysis patients have higher rates of allergic-like reactions

questions.explanation: Some nephrologists advocate more caution in peritoneal dialysis patients because residual urine output may be more important to their well-being than for patients on chronic hemodialysis. Any reduction in remaining urine output could have a more meaningful impact on fluid and solute management in this population.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following is listed as an indication for obtaining a serum creatinine before contrast administration?

choices.text: Age greater than 65 years
History of prior allergic-like contrast reaction
Diabetes mellitus
Obesity

questions.explanation: Suggested indications for obtaining a serum creatinine include a history of renal disease (dialysis, renal transplant, solitary kidney, renal cancer, or renal surgery), hypertension, and diabetes mellitus. Age alone, prior contrast reaction, and obesity are not among the listed indications. A creatinine value within 30 days of contrast administration is generally considered sufficient for at-risk patients with a stable clinical condition.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient with hypertension and diabetes had a serum creatinine drawn 45 days ago that was normal. Which of the following is most appropriate before contrast administration?

choices.text: Obtain a new serum creatinine
Proceed without repeat creatinine
Obtain creatinine only if additional CKD risk factors are present
Proceed without repeat creatinine only if the patient is hemodynamically stable

questions.explanation: For potentially at-risk patients, a creatinine value within 30 days of contrast administration is generally considered sufficient. A value obtained 45 days prior falls outside this window in a patient with both hypertension and diabetes - two listed indications for creatinine screening - and a repeat should be obtained before proceeding.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most widely accepted strategy for minimizing the risk of CI-AKI in at-risk patients?

choices.text: N-acetylcysteine orally before and after contrast
IV furosemide to promote diuresis before contrast
IV volume expansion with isotonic fluids
Sodium bicarbonate infusion prior to contrast

questions.explanation: The most widely accepted strategy for minimizing CI-AKI risk in at-risk patients (typically those with AKI or eGFR < 30) is IV volume expansion with isotonic fluids such as 0.9% saline or Lactated Ringer's solution. An example approach involves 100 mL/h for 6-12 hours before and 4-12 hours after contrast. No standard protocol has been established; volumes vary by patient and institutional guidelines.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following has been discredited as a means of preventing CI-AKI?

choices.text: 0.9% normal saline
Lactated Ringer's solution
N-acetylcysteine
Oral hydration with water

questions.explanation: N-acetylcysteine, mannitol, furosemide, and theophylline have all been discredited as means of preventing CI-AKI. Sodium bicarbonate solution has also been used but has not been shown to be more efficacious than saline or Lactated Ringer's for preventing AKI after IV contrast administration.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes is taking metformin and requires a contrast-enhanced CT. Her eGFR is 55 mL/min/1.73 m². Which of the following best describes the ACR's current recommendation?

choices.text: No precautions are necessary
Metformin should be withheld for 48 hours before contrast injection
Metformin should be withheld for 48 hours after contrast injection
Contrast is contraindicated in all patients taking metformin

questions.explanation: The ACR currently recommends no precautions for diabetic patients on metformin unless the patient has CKD with eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m², has AKI, or is undergoing arterial catheterization with renal artery emboli risk. There is no direct interaction between iodinated contrast and metformin. The concern is indirect - if AKI develops in a patient taking metformin, lactic acidosis becomes possible. With eGFR of 55 and no AKI, no precautions are needed.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: In which of the following scenarios should metformin be withheld for 48 hours after contrast administration and reinstituted only after renal function is reassessed?

choices.text: eGFR of 45-60 mL/min/1.73 m² with no other risk factors
History of prior allergic-like contrast reaction
Arterial catheterization with renal artery emboli risk
Age greater than 70 with diabetes mellitus

questions.explanation: Metformin should be withheld for 48 hours after contrast administration in patients with CKD and eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m², those with AKI, or those undergoing arterial catheterization with risk of emboli to the renal arteries. Metformin itself is not a risk factor for CI-AKI, but patients who develop renal failure while taking it are at risk for lactic acidosis given its 50% reported mortality rate in that setting.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the known fetal risks of intravascular iodinated contrast media?

choices.text: No evidence of harm to the fetus
Teratogenic in the first trimester; safe in second and third trimesters
Causes fetal thyroid suppression and should be avoided in all trimesters
Safe only when administered in the lowest possible dose at any gestational age

questions.explanation: Although iodinated contrast media cross the placenta, there is no evidence that maternal intravascular iodinated contrast exposure is harmful to the fetus. Specifically, there is no evidence that fetal exposure increases mutagenesis, fetal cancer risk, or adversely affects fetal renal or thyroid function. This is in contrast to gadolinium-based contrast media, which have shown adverse effects in animal fetuses.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: What percentage of maternally administered iodinated contrast media is ultimately absorbed through a breastfed infant's gastrointestinal tract?
questions.explanation: Only 1% of maternally administered contrast media enters breast milk, and of that, only 1% is absorbed through an infant's gastrointestinal tract - yielding approximately 0.01% of the administered maternal dose. This represents less than 1% of the recommended infant contrast dose and has no known adverse effect on the infant.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: What is the recommended guidance for a breastfeeding mother who has received iodinated contrast media?

choices.text: Breastfeeding must be suspended for at least 48 hours
Breastfeeding must be suspended for at least 24 hours
No precautions are generally necessary
Breastfeeding must be suspended for at least 1 week

questions.explanation: It is generally accepted that no precautions need to be taken, as the amount absorbed by the infant is negligible and has no known adverse effect. However, it is recommended that the mother be informed that studies assessing risks to infants are limited. If concerned, she may abstain from breastfeeding for 12 to 24 hours after the study and pump and discard milk produced during that time.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: The FDA updated thyroid function monitoring guidelines for young children who received iodinated contrast media in 2022. Which of the following best describes the current status of these guidelines?

choices.text: Controversial and not endorsed by the ACR Committee on Drugs and Contrast Media
Endorsed by the ACR Committee on Drugs and Contrast Media
Recommend routine thyroid testing in all children under 18 who receive contrast
Have been withdrawn by the FDA pending additional study

questions.explanation: In 2022, the FDA updated thyroid function monitoring guidelines for young children who received iodinated contrast media, recommending decisions be based on individualized assessment incorporating risk factors such as prematurity, very low birth weight, and other conditions affecting thyroid function. However, these guidelines remain controversial and have not been endorsed by the ACR Committee on Drugs and Contrast Media.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following is a recognized risk factor for contrast media extravasation?

choices.text: History of prior allergic-like contrast reaction
Injection in the antecubital fossa
Altered circulation in the injected extremity
Use of nonionic contrast media

questions.explanation: Extravasations are more common in patients who are uncommunicative, have altered circulation in the injected extremity, have had radiation to the injected extremity, or are injected in the hand, foot, or ankle. Injection into the antecubital or other large forearm veins is actually preferred to reduce extravasation risk.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT recommended to help reduce the risk of contrast extravasation?

choices.text: Using angiocatheters for contrast injection
Confirming line position via blood aspiration
Injecting in the wrist or hand
Performing a small test injection

questions.explanation: Methods to reduce extravasation risk include using angiocatheters instead of butterfly needles, confirming line position via blood aspiration, performing a small test injection, and carefully securing the catheter. Injections into the antecubital or other large forearm veins are preferred over the hand, wrist, foot, or ankle.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the effectiveness of local interventions after contrast extravasation has occurred?

choices.text: Aspiration of extravasated media is the most effective intervention
Injection of corticosteroids into the site significantly reduces tissue injury
Elevation and warm or cold compresses are recommended
Hyaluronidase injection is the most effective treatment for compartment syndrome risk

questions.explanation: Little can be done to mitigate the effects of contrast extravasation after it occurs. Elevation of the affected extremity above heart level is recommended to reduce capillary hydrostatic pressure and promote resorption. Cold or warm compresses may be applied. Attempted aspiration of extravasated contrast and injection of medications such as corticosteroids or hyaluronidase into the extravasation site are ineffective.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following findings after contrast extravasation is an indication for prompt surgical consultation?

choices.text: Erythema at the injection site with intact skin
Pain and swelling immediately after extravasation
Change in sensation or parasthesia
Any extravasation in a patient with diabetes mellitus

questions.explanation: Surgical consultation should be obtained when there is concern for a developing compartment syndrome or tissue necrosis. Ominous symptoms requiring prompt surgical consultation include progressive swelling or pain, decreased active or passive range of motion, altered tissue perfusion (decreased capillary refill), change in sensation or paresthesia, and skin ulceration or blistering. The earliest and most reliable sign of severe injury is severe or progressive pain.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: At what volume of contrast extravasation is surgical consultation considered mandatory?

choices.text: 10 mL
30 mL
50 mL
There is no volume threshold above which surgical consultation is considered mandatory

questions.explanation: There is no extravasation volume threshold above which surgical consultation is considered mandatory. The decision to obtain surgical consultation is based on clinical findings - specifically the presence of ominous symptoms such as progressive swelling or pain, decreased range of motion, altered tissue perfusion, neurologic changes, or skin ulceration - not on the volume extravasated.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following is true regarding the structure of macrocyclic and linear gadolinium-based contrast media?

choices.text: In macrocyclic agents, the chelate forms a ring that surrounds the gadolinium ion
Macrocyclic agents have a longer molecular chain that binds gadolinium at multiple sites
Linear agents encage the gadolinium ion within a ring structure, providing greater stability
Macrocyclic and linear agents differ only in molecular weight, not in chelate structure

questions.explanation: Gadolinium-based contrast media are classified as macrocyclic or linear based on the shape of the chelate that binds the gadolinium ion. In macrocyclic agents, the chelate forms a ring that encages the gadolinium ion, resulting in more stable binding. In linear agents, the chelate is not in ring form, resulting in less stable gadolinium binding. This structural difference has direct implications for gadolinium release (transmetallation) and NSF risk.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Among linear gadolinium-based contrast media, which subtype has the least stable gadolinium binding?

choices.text: Nonionic linear agents
Ionic linear agents
Both ionic and nonionic linear agents have equivalent stability
Stability is determined by dose rather than ionicity

questions.explanation: Among linear agents, the nonionic agents are less stable than the ionic agents in terms of gadolinium binding to the chelate. The overall hierarchy of stability is: nonionic linear < ionic linear < macrocyclic. This is clinically relevant - two of the three highest-risk agents for NSF (Gadodiamide (Omniscan) and gadoversetamide (OptiMark)) are nonionic linear agents.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly classifies gadodiamide (Omniscan)?

choices.text: Ionic, linear
Nonionic, macrocyclic
Ionic, macrocyclic
Nonionic, linear

questions.explanation: Gadodiamide (Omniscan) is a nonionic, linear GBCM. It is one of the three highest-risk agents for NSF development, the other two being gadoversetamide (OptiMark), and gadopentetate dimeglumine (Magnevist). Nonionic linear agents have the least stable gadolinium binding among all GBCM classes, which is central to the theoretical mechanism of NSF via transmetallation.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Gadoterate meglumine (Dotarem/Clariscan) is best classified as which of the following?

choices.text: Nonionic, linear
Ionic, linear
Nonionic, macrocyclic
Ionic, macrocyclic

questions.explanation: Gadoterate meglumine (Dotarem/Clariscan) is an ionic, macrocyclic agent. It belongs to the lower-risk group for NSF. Macrocyclic agents, regardless of ionicity, have more stable gadolinium binding than linear agents due to the ring structure of their chelate.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Compared to iodinated contrast media, acute adverse reactions to gadolinium-based contrast media occur at approximately what frequency?

choices.text: Two to four times more frequently
At a similar frequency
Ten times less frequently
Two to four times less frequently

questions.explanation: Acute adverse reactions to GBCM occur approximately two to four times less frequently than reactions to iodinated contrast media. The majority of GBCM reactions are mild and physiologic in nature, including coldness at the injection site, nausea, headache, warmth, paresthesias, and dizziness. Fatal reactions have been reported but are exceedingly rare.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most frequently occurring allergic-like symptom after gadolinium-based contrast media administration?

choices.text: Bronchospasm
Laryngeal edema
Rash, hives, or urticaria
Cardiovascular collapse

questions.explanation: Rash, hives, and urticaria are the most frequent allergic-like symptoms after GBCM administration. Respiratory and cardiovascular reactions can occur but are less common. The clear majority of GBCM reactions are mild and non-allergic (physiologic) in character.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient undergoing a gadolinium-enhanced liver MRI develops transient tachypnea during arterial phase image acquisition. Which contrast agent is most likely responsible?

choices.text: Gadoxetate disodium (Eovist)
Gadobutrol (Gadavist)
Gadoteridol (ProHance)
Gadoterate meglumine (Dotarem)

questions.explanation: Transient tachypnea is a unique physiologic side effect associated specifically with gadoxetate disodium (Eovist). It can cause motion artifact during arterial-phase MRI acquisitions and is more common with high-volume, off-label administrations.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following represents the single greatest risk factor for an adverse reaction to gadolinium-based contrast media?

choices.text: History of asthma
Multiple food allergies
Prior allergic-like reaction to iodinated contrast media
Prior allergic-like reaction to any GBCM

questions.explanation: The highest risk factor for an adverse reaction to GBCM is a prior allergic-like reaction to GBCM - even to a different GBCM agent. Other risk factors include allergies in general and asthma. Notably, a prior reaction to iodinated contrast media is not believed to increase the risk of a GBCM reaction above that of other allergies.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient with a history of severe anaphylaxis to iodinated contrast media is referred for a contrast-enhanced MRI. How does this history affect the risk of an adverse reaction to gadolinium-based contrast media?

choices.text: It does not increase the risk above that of other allergies
It significantly increases the risk and requires premedication
It is considered an absolute contraindication to GBCM
It doubles the baseline risk of a GBCM reaction

questions.explanation: A prior allergic-like reaction to iodinated contrast media is not believed to increase the risk of an allergic-like reaction to GBCM above that of other allergies. This is an important clinical distinction - only a prior reaction specifically to GBCM confers the highest level of risk for a subsequent GBCM reaction.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient with a prior allergic-like reaction to gadobutrol (Gadavist) requires contrast-enhanced MRI. Which of the following is an appropriate preventive measure?

choices.text: Administer gadobutrol at half the standard dose
Avoid all gadolinium-based agents permanently
Use a different gadolinium compound for reinjection
Premedicate and use the same agent at a standard dose

questions.explanation: One recommended preventive measure for patients with a prior adverse reaction to GBCM is to use a different gadolinium compound for reinjection. Additionally, premedication with corticosteroids and antihistamines may be considered, using a regimen identical to that used for prophylaxis of iodinated contrast reactions, though its effectiveness for GBCM has not yet been confirmed.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which gadolinium-based contrast media is contraindicated in patients who have had prior allergic-like reaction to gadolinium-based contrast media?

choices.text: Gadobenate dimeglumine (MultiHance)
Gadodiamide (Omniscan)
Gadoterate meglumine (Dotarem)
Gadopiclenol (Elucirem)

questions.explanation: The FDA-approved package insert for gadobenate dimeglumine (MultiHance) specifically states that this agent is contraindicated in patients who have had any prior allergic-like contrast reaction. This is a unique labeling distinction among available GBCM agents.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: What is the current evidence base for premedication prior to gadolinium-based contrast media administration in high-risk patients?

choices.text: Evidence has been extrapolated from iodinated contrast media experience
Multiple randomized controlled trials confirm its effectiveness for GBCM
Current guidelines recommend against premedication for GBCM
Premedication has been shown to be ineffective in prospective GBCM studies

questions.explanation: The effectiveness of premedication before GBCM administration has not yet been determined in controlled studies. Premedication is still sometimes performed, based on evidence extrapolated from experience with iodinated contrast media, using a regimen identical to that used for prophylaxis of adverse reactions to iodinated contrast.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Gadolinium-based contrast media are classified by the FDA as pregnancy category C. Which of the following best describes the physiologic basis for their relative contraindication in pregnancy?

choices.text: GBCM may persist in the fetal circulation for a prolonged period
GBCM are directly teratogenic to fetal neural tissue during organogenesis
GBCM accumulate in the placenta and impair uteroplacental blood flow
GBCM cause irreversible fetal renal tubular toxicity

questions.explanation: GBCM cross the placental barrier, enter fetal circulation, are filtered by the fetal kidneys, and are excreted into the amniotic fluid where they may remain for a prolonged period. This prolonged presence in amniotic fluid could theoretically increase the risk of gadolinium dissociation from its chelate and precipitation in fetal tissue. No adequate and well-controlled studies in humans have been performed; animal studies have shown adverse fetal effects.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the recommended approach to gadolinium-based contrast media administration in pregnant patients?

choices.text: GBCM should only be administered when the benefit is thought to outweigh the potential risk
GBCM are absolutely contraindicated throughout all trimesters of pregnancy
GBCM are safe and can be administered freely after the first trimester
GBCM require special FDA authorization before use in a pregnant patient

questions.explanation: GBCM are classified as FDA pregnancy category C - relatively, not absolutely, contraindicated. They should only be administered in pregnant patients in carefully selected situations where the benefit is thought to outweigh the potential risk. A serious risk-benefit discussion is warranted given the theoretical concern about prolonged gadolinium retention in amniotic fluid.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: What percentage of administered gadolinium-based contrast media is excreted into the breast milk of breastfeeding mothers?
questions.explanation: Only 0.04% of administered GBCM is excreted into the milk of breastfeeding mothers. Of this already tiny amount, only 1% is absorbed through the infant's gastrointestinal tract. This is much less than the allowed GBCM dose when a contrast-enhanced study is needed in an infant, and there is no evidence that the tiny absorbed amount has any adverse effect on the breastfed infant.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: What is the recommended approach to breastfeeding after a contrast-enhanced MRI?

choices.text: There is no need to stop breastfeeding
Breastfeeding must be discontinued for 48 hours
Breastfeeding must be discontinued for 12 to 24 hours and milk discarded
The infant should be observed for rash and GI symptoms for 24 hours after the first feeding

questions.explanation: Because only 0.04% of GBCM is excreted into breast milk and only 1% of that is absorbed through the infant's GI tract - with no evidence of any adverse effect on breastfed infants - there is no need to stop breastfeeding after a GBCM-enhanced study. However, if the mother remains concerned despite counseling, she may choose to pump and discard milk produced in the 12 to 24 hours following the study.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A breastfeeding mother has received gadolinium-based contrast media and remains concerned about possible infant exposure despite being counseled that breastfeeding is safe to continue. What is the appropriate guidance?

choices.text: She may pump and discard milk produced in the 12 to 24 hours following the study
She must pump and discard all milk for 48 hours
Breastfeeding should be stopped for one week as a precaution
No options other than resuming normal breastfeeding are appropriate

questions.explanation: Explanation: While evidence does not support the need to interrupt breastfeeding after GBCM administration, a concerned mother may choose to pump and discard milk produced during the 12 to 24 hours following the study. This represents an optional precaution - not a clinical necessity - for mothers who remain concerned after being informed of the available evidence.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient with severe CKD exposed to gadodiamide (Omniscan) several years ago presents with progressive skin thickening, plaque formation of the extremities, and joint immobility. What is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.text: Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis
Gadolinium retention syndrome
Contrast-induced nephropathy
Systemic sclerosis from an unrelated cause

questions.explanation: The described presentation is consistent with nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF), a fibrosing disease most evident in the skin and subcutaneous tissues that can also involve the lungs, esophagus, heart, and skeletal muscles. Initial symptoms typically include skin thickening with plaque formation, potentially progressing to contractures and joint immobility. NSF occurs nearly exclusively in patients with severe CKD or AKI who have been exposed to GBCM.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the prognosis and available treatment for nephrogenic systemic fibrosis?

choices.text: The disease may be fatal and there is no known effective treatment
Most cases resolve fully with prolonged corticosteroid therapy
The disease is self-limited and typically resolves within 6 to 12 months
Chelation therapy reliably reverses NSF if initiated early

questions.explanation: NSF is a serious and potentially fatal condition. Symptoms and signs may progress rapidly, with some patients developing contractures and joint immobility. There is no known effective treatment. The absence of any effective therapy makes prevention - through appropriate patient screening and avoidance of high-risk agents - the critical priority.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Below which eGFR threshold are the three highest-risk gadolinium-based contrast media absolutely contraindicated by the FDA?

choices.text: eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m²
eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m²
eGFR < 45 mL/min/1.73 m²
eGFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m²

questions.explanation: The three highest-risk GBCM - gadodiamide (Omniscan), gadoversetamide (OptiMark), and gadopentetate dimeglumine (Magnevist) - are absolutely contraindicated by the FDA in patients with an eGFR less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m². NSF occurs nearly exclusively in patients with severe CKD meeting this threshold or in patients with AKI.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly identifies the three gadolinium-based contrast media agents at highest risk for NSF?

choices.text: Gadopentetate dimeglumine (Magnevist), gadodiamide (Omniscan), and gadoversetamide (OptiMark)
Gadobenate dimeglumine (MultiHance), gadodiamide (Omniscan), and gadobutrol (Gadavist)
Gadoterate meglumine (Dotarem), gadopentetate dimeglumine (Magnevist), and gadodiamide (Omniscan)
Gadoxetate disodium (Eovist), gadodiamide (Omniscan), and gadoversetamide (OptiMark)

questions.explanation: The three highest-risk GBCM for NSF are gadopentetate dimeglumine (Magnevist), gadodiamide (Omniscan), and gadoversetamide (OptiMark, no longer manufactured). These agents are absolutely contraindicated by the FDA in patients with eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m² or AKI. Institutions using these agents should screen patients referred for contrast-enhanced MRI for renal disease.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient with an eGFR of 22 mL/min/1.73 m² requires contrast-enhanced MRI. Assuming a contrast-enhanced scan is necessary, which of the following agents would be the safest to use in this situation?

choices.text: Gadodiamide (Omniscan)
Gadopentetate dimeglumine (Magnevist)
Gadoversetamide (OptiMark)
Gadobutrol (Gadavist)

questions.explanation: Gadobutrol (Gadavist) is a macrocyclic, lower-risk GBCM agent. Few, if any, cases of unconfounded NSF have been reported with the lower-risk agents, which include gadobenate dimeglumine (MultiHance), gadobutrol (Gadavist), gadoterate meglumine (Dotarem/Clariscan), and gadoteridol (ProHance). The other answer choices - Omniscan, Magnevist, and OptiMark - are absolutely contraindicated at this eGFR.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between gadolinium-based contrast media dose and NSF risk?

choices.text: Higher and multiple doses of higher-risk GBCM increase the likelihood of NSF
NSF risk is not related to dose or number of administrations
NSF only occurs after more than three administrations of a high-risk agent
NSF risk is associated with higher doses of GBCM but not associated with the number of administrations

questions.explanation: Higher doses and multiple doses of the higher-risk GBCM are believed to increase the likelihood of NSF developing. However, cases have occurred after only a single administration of a standard dose of a high-risk agent, underscoring that no exposure is entirely without risk in susceptible patients.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: What is the speculated mechanism by which high-risk gadolinium-based contrast media are thought to cause NSF?

choices.text: Dissociation of the gadolinium ion from its chelate with subsequent precipitation in tissue
Direct cytotoxicity of the chelate molecule on dermal fibroblasts
Immune complex deposition in dermal vasculature triggered by gadolinium
Gadolinium-mediated complement activation and mast cell degranulation

questions.explanation: The mechanism of NSF is unknown, but the leading speculation is that gadolinium dissociates from its chelate in vivo - a process called transmetallation, in which a different body ion displaces and releases the gadolinium atom. The freed gadolinium then precipitates in tissue. This hypothesis is supported by the fact that the three high-risk GBCM have lower stability of gadolinium binding to the chelate and are therefore more susceptible to this process.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following is a newer gadolinium-based contrast media agents which is associated with limited evidence regarding NSF but has been found to carry a very low risk?

choices.text: Gadodiamide (Omniscan)
Gadobenate dimeglumine (MultiHance)
Gadoversetamide (OptiMark)
Gadoxetate disodium (Eovist)

questions.explanation: Gadoxetate disodium (Eovist) is a newer agent with limited information about its association with NSF. However, the risk of NSF developing after its administration has been found to be very low. The lower-risk group with more established evidence includes MultiHance, Gadavist, Dotarem/Clariscan, and ProHance.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Gadopiclenol (Elucirem/Vueway) was approved by the FDA in 2022. Which of the following correctly describes a distinguishing property of this gadolinium-based contrast agent?

choices.text: It is a linear, ionic agent with lower gadolinium retention in the brain
It is the only GBCM safe to administer when eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m²
It is the only ionic macrocyclic agent currently available in the United States
It is a macrocyclic agent approved at half the standard dose

questions.explanation: Gadopiclenol (Elucirem/Vueway), approved by the FDA in 2022, is a macrocyclic agent in the lower-risk NSF group. It has the highest relaxivity values of any GBCM approved in the US. Based on non-inferiority trials, it was approved at a dose of 0.05 mmol/kg - half the dose of most other agents (0.1 mmol/kg) - resulting in a 50% reduction in the total amount of gadolinium administered.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Gadolinium retention in the body after gadolinium-based contrast media administration has been identified in which locations?

choices.text: The liver and spleen
The skeleton
The brain
The skeleton and brain

questions.explanation: Gadolinium retention occurs in the skeleton - a long-established finding - and more recently has been identified in the brain, specifically in the globus pallidus and dentate nucleus. Brain retention occurs even in patients with normal renal function. The amount of retention is proportional to the cumulative GBCM received and is greater with linear than macrocyclic agents.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Regarding gadolinium accumulation in the brain, which of the following is accurate?

choices.text: Brain retention is greater with macrocyclic than linear agents
Brain retention occurs only in patients with severe CKD
Gadolinium retention in the brain has been shown to cause measurable cognitive decline
No adverse neurologic effects have been identified

questions.explanation: There is currently no evidence of any adverse neurologic effects from gadolinium deposition in the brain, even after millions of GBCM administrations worldwide. However, further study is necessary to determine whether this deposition has any long-term consequences. Retention is greater with linear than macrocyclic agents and occurs regardless of renal function.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: When a contrast reaction occurs, a responding radiologist should quickly obtain key information. Which of the following is the LEAST important piece of information to be ascertained?

choices.text: The reason for the imaging study
The patient's current symptoms
A summary of the patient's health problems and medications
The time of the patient's last oral intake and the contrast volume administered

questions.explanation: When a contrast reaction occurs, a brief discussion with the patient and any present healthcare providers should provide: the reason for the imaging study, a description of the patient's current symptoms, and a summary of the patient's health problems and medications. Vital signs should be obtained promptly, IV access secured, a pulse oximeter made available, and oxygen made available.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT part of the initial assessment a radiologist should perform when evaluating the severity of a contrast reaction?

choices.text: Determine the level of patient consciousness
Determine the presence or absence of respiratory and cardiovascular symptoms
Assess the appearance of the skin
Administer diphenhydramine and epinephrine simultaneously

questions.explanation: The examining radiologist should quickly determine the level of patient consciousness, the appearance of the skin, the quality of phonation, and the presence or absence of respiratory and cardiovascular symptoms. This rapid assessment guides the aggressiveness of subsequent management, which depends on the type and severity of the reaction.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Epinephrine for contrast reactions is available in two concentrations. Which of the following correctly describes the appropriate clinical use of each formulation?

choices.text: 1 mg/1 mL for IM; 1 mg/10 mL for IV
1 mg/1 mL for IV; 1 mg/10 mL for IM
Both formulations are appropriate for IM use only
Formulations are interchangeable for IM and IV use

questions.explanation: The concentrated 1 mg/mL formulation in a 1 mL vial is intended for intramuscular injection only. The more dilute 1 mg/10 mL (0.1 mg/mL) formulation is intended for intravenous use as a slow IV push into a running infusion of fluids. Both contain the same total dose of 1 mg but in different volumes - a frequent source of clinical confusion since both may be stocked in code carts.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A contrast reaction occurs in a patient without IV access. What is the appropriate route of epinephrine?

choices.text: Subcutaneous
Intravenous
Sublingual
Intramuscular

questions.explanation: In the absence of IV access, IM epinephrine is the first-line intervention. The appropriate dose is 0.3 mL of the 1 mg/mL formulation (0.3 mg), or an IM EpiPen or equivalent (0.3 mL). IV epinephrine should be reserved for patients who are severely unstable and already have a running IV line. IM epinephrine may be repeated up to a total of 1 mg.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient develops mild urticaria without respiratory or cardiovascular symptoms after gadolinium-based contrast media administration. What is the most appropriate next step?

choices.text: Administer IV diphenhydramine 50 mg immediately
Administer IM epinephrine 0.3 mg
Transfer to the emergency department
No immediate treatment is needed

questions.explanation: For hives (urticaria), no treatment is needed in most cases. If symptomatic, diphenhydramine (Benadryl) 25 to 50 mg orally, intramuscularly, or intravenously may be given, or fexofenadine (Allegra) 180 mg PO. Epinephrine and emergency transfer are not indicated for isolated urticaria without systemic signs.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient develops diffuse erythema after gadolinium-based contrast media administration. Blood pressure is 124/80 mmHg and SpO₂ is 99%. After preserving IV access and initiating oxygen, what is the most appropriate next step?

choices.text: Give 1 L of IV normal saline rapidly
Administer IM epinephrine 0.3 mg
Administer IV diphenhydramine 50 mg
No further treatment is usually needed

questions.explanation: For diffuse erythema with a normotensive patient, no further treatment beyond preserving IV access, monitoring vitals, and administering oxygen is usually needed. Antihistamines should be used with caution in this setting, as they may exacerbate existing or developing hypotension. The patient should continue to be monitored for any progression of symptoms.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient develops diffuse erythema and a blood pressure of 76/48 mmHg after contrast administration. IV access is in place. After initiating oxygen and monitoring, what is the most appropriate next step?

choices.text: Administer diphenhydramine 50 mg IV
Administer IM epinephrine 0.3 mg immediately
Elevate the head of the bed and observe
Give 1 L of IV fluids rapidly

questions.explanation: For diffuse erythema with hypotension, after securing IV access, monitoring vitals, and initiating oxygen, the next step is to rapidly give 1 L of IV fluids (0.9% normal saline or Lactated Ringer's). If hypotension is profound or does not respond to IV fluids, IV epinephrine (1 mg/10 mL, 1 mL = 0.1 mg) slowly into a running infusion should then be considered.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient develops progressive hoarseness and stridor after contrast administration. IV access is secured, monitoring is underway, and oxygen has been initiated. What is the most appropriate next step?

choices.text: Administer albuterol 2 puffs via inhaler
Administer diphenhydramine
Administer atropine
Administer epinephrine IM

questions.explanation: For laryngeal edema, after the initial steps of securing IV access, monitoring vitals, and administering oxygen, epinephrine should be given - either IM (1 mg/mL, 0.3 mL = 0.3 mg) or via IM EpiPen or equivalent. If the patient is also hypotensive, IV epinephrine (1 mg/10 mL, 1 mL slowly into a running infusion) may be used. Epinephrine may be repeated as needed up to a maximum total dose of 1 mg.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient develops bronchospasm with audible wheezing and dyspnea after contrast administration. Vital signs are stable. IV access is secured, monitoring is underway, and oxygen has been initiated. What is the most appropriate next pharmacologic step?

choices.text: Epinephrine IM
Diphenhydramine IV
Atropine IV
Albuterol beta-agonist inhaler

questions.explanation: For bronchospasm, the first pharmacologic intervention after initial supportive steps is a beta-agonist inhaler - albuterol 2 puffs (90 mcg per puff), which can be repeated up to three times. If bronchospasm is severe or unresponsive to the inhaler, epinephrine should be added: IM (1 mg/mL, 0.3 mL) or IM EpiPen, or IV epinephrine (1 mg/10 mL) if the patient has a running IV line.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient develops hypotension after contrast administration. Which of the following is included in the appropriate initial management of hypotension from any cause?

choices.text: Administer atropine 0.6 mg IV immediately and elevate the patient's legs
Administer IV epinephrine immediately
Place the patient in reverse Trendelenburg position and administer IV fluids
Elevate legs, administer oxygen, and consider 1 L IV fluids

questions.explanation: For hypotension from any cause (SBP < 90 mmHg), initial management includes preserving IV access, monitoring vitals with a pulse oximeter, elevating the legs at least 60 degrees (Trendelenburg position), administering oxygen at 6 to 10 L/min via mask, and considering rapid administration of 1 L of IV fluids (0.9% normal saline or Lactated Ringer's).

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient develops hypotension with a pulse of 44 bpm following contrast administration. Initial supportive measures have been started but the patient remains unresponsive to them. What is the most appropriate pharmacologic next step?

choices.text: Epinephrine IM 0.3 mg
Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV
Methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg IV
Atropine 0.6 mg IV

questions.explanation: In a vagal reaction (hypotension with bradycardia, pulse < 60 bpm) that is severe and unresponsive to initial supportive measures, atropine 0.6 to 1.0 mg IV into a running infusion of IV fluids is the appropriate pharmacologic intervention. It may be repeated up to a maximum total dose of 3 mg. Note that lower doses of atropine may paradoxically exacerbate bradycardia.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient develops hypotension (SBP 80 mmHg) with a pulse of 124 bpm following contrast administration. After initial supportive measures, the patient remains hypotensive. What is the most appropriate next step?

choices.text: Atropine
Albuterol inhaler
Methylprednisolone
Epinephrine

questions.explanation: Hypotension with tachycardia (pulse > 100 bpm) is consistent with an allergic-like reaction rather than a vagal reaction. If hypotension persists after basic supportive treatment, the appropriate next step is IM epinephrine 0.3 mL (0.3 mg) of 1 mg/mL solution, or IM EpiPen or equivalent. If unresponsive to IM dosing, IV epinephrine (1 mg/10 mL, 1 mL into a running infusion) may then be given.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A contrast reaction patient becomes unresponsive and pulseless. What is the appropriate sequence of immediate actions?

choices.text: Administer epinephrine IM immediately, then activate emergency response
Establish IV access, then administer epinephrine IV and begin CPR
Defibrillate immediately
Check for responsiveness, call 911, and perform CPR

questions.explanation: For an unresponsive and pulseless patient, the sequence is: check for responsiveness, activate the emergency response team or call 911, and perform CPR per American Heart Association protocols. Defibrillation should be performed as indicated if equipment is available. Epinephrine IV (1 mg/10 mL, full 10 mL = 1 mg dose) may be administered between 2-minute cycles of CPR.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following accurately describes the role of IV corticosteroids in the management of contrast reactions?

choices.text: IV corticosteroids are the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis and should be given immediately
IV corticosteroids are useful acutely but must be given within 15 minutes to be effective
IV corticosteroids are contraindicated in contrast reactions because they can mask symptom progression
IV corticosteroids are not useful in acute treatment but may help prevent short-term allergic-like reaction recurrence

questions.explanation: IV corticosteroids are not useful in the acute treatment of any contrast reaction. However, they may help prevent a short-term recurrence of an allergic-like reaction and may be considered before transport to the emergency department in a patient who has had a severe allergic-like reaction. Appropriate agents include hydrocortisone 5 mg/kg IV or methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg IV, administered over 1 to 2 minutes.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient has a mild contrast reaction that resolves spontaneously within 10 minutes. What is the most appropriate post-reaction monitoring approach?

choices.text: The patient may be discharged immediately since the reaction has resolved
The patient should be admitted for 24-hour inpatient observation
No monitoring is needed if the reaction was classified as physiologic rather than allergic
All patients should be monitored until their symptoms have improved

questions.explanation: Mild reactions usually resolve within 20 to 30 minutes and do not require medical treatment; however, all patients should be monitored until their symptoms have improved. This is because some patients who ultimately develop moderate or severe reactions may initially present with only mild symptoms, and the clinical trajectory must be followed closely.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A 25 kg child develops bronchospasm following contrast administration. After initial supportive steps, what is the appropriate albuterol dose?

choices.text: 1 puff (90 mcg); repeat doses are contraindicated in children under 30 kg
4 puffs (90 mcg per puff) for a total of 360 mcg; may repeat once
Albuterol is not recommended in pediatric contrast reactions
2 puffs (90 mcg per puff) for a total of 180 mcg

questions.explanation: Pediatric albuterol dosing for contrast reactions is identical to that in adults: 2 puffs (90 mcg per puff) for a total of 180 mcg, which may be repeated up to three times. Weight-based modification is not required for inhaled albuterol in this setting.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A 20 kg child requires diphenhydramine for symptomatic urticaria following a contrast reaction. What is the appropriate dose?

choices.text: 25 mg flat dose regardless of weight
2 mg/kg up to a maximum of 50 mg
0.5 mg/kg up to a maximum of 25 mg
1 mg/kg up to a maximum of 50 mg

questions.explanation: Pediatric diphenhydramine (Benadryl) dosing for contrast reactions is 1 mg/kg up to a maximum of 50 mg. For a 20 kg child, this would be 20 mg. The adult dose of 25 to 50 mg is not appropriate to use as a flat pediatric dose without weight-based calculation.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A 22 kg child requires epinephrine for an allergic-like contrast reaction. Which of the following represents the most appropriate initial IM epinephrine approach?

choices.text: 0.3 mg epinephrine IM
0.1 mg epinephrine IM
Epinephrine is contraindicated in children under 30 kg
0.15 mg epinephrine IM

questions.explanation: For patients weighing up to 30 kg, EpiPen Jr (0.15 mL of 1 mg/mL = 0.15 mg) is appropriate for IM dosing as a single dose. For patients over 30 kg, the adult EpiPen (0.3 mg) or weight-based dosing (0.01 mg/kg of 1 mg/mL, maximum single dose 0.3 mg) is used. IM epinephrine may be repeated every 5 to 15 minutes as needed up to a maximum dose of 1 mg.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A 15 kg child requires IV fluid resuscitation during a contrast reaction. What is the appropriate initial fluid dose?

choices.text: 5 to 10 mL/kg, up to 500 to 1000 mL maximum
30 mL/kg as a fixed bolus
1 L as the standard dose, regardless of weight
10 to 20 mL/kg, up to 500 to 1000 mL maximum

questions.explanation: Pediatric isotonic fluid dosing during contrast reactions is 10 to 20 mL/kg of 0.9% normal saline or Lactated Ringer's, up to a maximum volume of 500 to 1000 mL. For a 15 kg child, this corresponds to 150 to 300 mL as the initial bolus.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 4: Practical Safety Applications in Radiology
questions.stem: A 20 kg child requires IV epinephrine for a severe contrast reaction with existing IV access. What is the maximum single IV epinephrine dose?

choices.text: 0.2 mg (2 mL of 1 mg/10 mL solution)
0.02 mg (0.2 mL of 1 mg/10 mL solution)
0.3 mg (3 mL of 1 mg/10 mL solution)
0.1 mg (1 mL of 1 mg/10 mL solution)

questions.explanation: Pediatric IV epinephrine dosing is 0.1 mL/kg (0.01 mg/kg) of the 1 mg/10 mL solution, with a maximum single dose of 1 mL (0.1 mg). For a 20 kg child, the weight-based calculation yields 2 mL, but the dose is capped at the maximum single dose of 1 mL (0.1 mg). This may be repeated every 5 to 15 minutes as needed up to a maximum total dose of 1 mg (10 mL).

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of a Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) code?

choices.text: To identify the diagnosing physician and referring institution for insurance purposes
To assign a unique identifier to each medical service or procedure
To establish a patient's diagnosis for insurance documentation
To communicate imaging findings between radiologists and clinical providers

questions.explanation: Each service or procedure that a physician provides is given a unique CPT code, which in turn is assigned a specific reimbursement amount. CPT codes are assigned based on the specific details of the described service. The CPT code set is maintained by the AMA CPT Editorial Panel, which authorizes new codes, modifies existing codes, and deletes codes no longer relevant.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the primary responsibility of the AMA CPT Editorial Panel?

choices.text: Setting the dollar value of reimbursement for each CPT code
Maintaining the CPT code set, including authorizing new codes, modifying existing codes, and deleting obsolete codes
Submitting reimbursement claims to Medicare on behalf of radiology practices
Reviewing malpractice claims related to billing errors

questions.explanation: The American Medical Association (AMA) CPT Editorial Panel is responsible for maintaining the CPT code set, including authorizing new codes, modifying existing codes, and deleting codes no longer relevant. A separate committee - the AMA CPT Advisory Committee - assists the Editorial Panel by making recommendations regarding new and existing codes.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the composition of the CPT Advisory Committee?

choices.text: CMS administrators and Medicare payment specialists
Representatives nominated by national medical societies
Elected members of the AMA Board of Trustees
Hospital administrators and healthcare compliance officers

questions.explanation: The CPT Advisory Committee is composed of representatives nominated by national medical societies. For example, national radiology societies designate representatives to the CPT Advisory Committee, who then advocate for radiologists by making recommendations for new or existing radiology CPT codes. This is distinct from the CPT Editorial Panel itself, which the Advisory Committee supports.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: Which body ultimately sets the valuation of RVUs for each CPT code?

choices.text: The AMA RBRVS Update Committee (RUC)
The AMA CPT Editorial Panel
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS)
The American College of Radiology

questions.explanation: Although the AMA RBRVS Update Committee (RUC) makes recommendations to CMS for RVU valuation for each CPT code, CMS ultimately sets the valuation of RVUs. CMS has historically accepted AMA RUC recommendations in the vast majority of cases. The RUC is predominantly composed of physicians representing various medical societies.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A radiology group uses work RVUs (wRVUs) to track physician productivity. Which component of the total RVU does the wRVU represent?

choices.text: Costs of maintaining the practice, including equipment and nonphysician staff
Professional liability (malpractice) expenses
Encounter time, intensity, effort, and skill
The conversion factor applied to determine actual reimbursement

questions.explanation: An RVU assigned to each CPT code reflects three components: 1) the work RVU (wRVU) - encounter time, intensity, effort, and skill; 2) the practice expense RVU - costs of maintaining a practice such as equipment, supplies, and nonphysician staff; and 3) the malpractice RVU - professional liability expenses. Actual reimbursement is calculated by multiplying the total RVU by the Conversion Factor (CF), which is set annually by CMS.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: CMS defines medical necessity as healthcare services or supplies that meet which of the following criteria?

choices.text: Services ordered by a board-certified physician for a patient with an active insurance policy
Services needed to prevent, diagnose, or treat an illness, injury, condition, or disease, and that meet accepted standards of medicine
Any service that has been assigned a valid CPT code by the AMA
Services for which preauthorization has been obtained from the insurer

questions.explanation: CMS defines medical necessity as "healthcare services or supplies needed to prevent, diagnose, or treat an illness, injury, condition, disease, or its symptoms and that meet accepted standards of medicine." In practice, the medical necessity determination is usually a rules-based administrative exercise at the time a claim is submitted, wherein a CPT service code must match a pre-approved ICD-10 diagnosis code.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the role of professional medical coders in radiology reimbursement?

choices.text: They determine the conversion factor used to calculate reimbursement
They extract information from radiology reports for billing purposes
They review and approve preauthorization requests submitted by ordering physicians
They audit malpractice claims and recommend institutional compliance plans

questions.explanation: Professional coders, assisted by software tools, extract information from radiology reports to assign both ICD-10 and CPT codes. They extract information from: 1) the examination indication and clinical history provided by the referring physician or patient; and 2) specific diagnostic information located in the findings section, or preferably the impression section, of the radiologist's report. The Radiology Coding Certification Board is the primary organization that credentials professional imaging coders.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: For CT and MRI examinations, what is the primary determinant of the appropriate CPT code?

choices.text: The body part imaged
The number of images acquired during the study
Whether or not contrast was administered
The clinical indication provided by the referring physician

questions.explanation: For CT and MRI, the details of contrast administration - without contrast, with contrast, or without and with contrast - determine the CPT code for a specific body part. For radiography, more views generally translate to higher complexity codes. For ultrasound, organ inventory checklists apply to abdominal, pelvic, obstetrical, and extremity imaging.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient with known coronary artery disease is scheduled for an elective outpatient cardiac MRI at a freestanding imaging center. The insurer contracts with a radiology benefit management (RBM) company. Which of the following is most accurate regarding preauthorization?

choices.text: Preauthorization is not typically required for MRI
Preauthorization is required, and approval by the RBM guarantees a subsequent favorable medical necessity determination
Preauthorization may be required, but approval by the RBM does not guarantee a subsequent favorable medical necessity determination
Preauthorization requirements apply only to inpatient and emergency department services

questions.explanation: Many private payers, Medicaid plans, and Medicare Advantage plans contract with radiology benefit management (RBM) companies and require preauthorization for elective outpatient advanced imaging services. However, preauthorization by the RBM does not always guarantee a subsequent favorable medical necessity determination by the insurer when the claim is filed. Preauthorization requirements generally do not apply to emergency department and inpatient services.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of Clinical Decision Support (CDS) software in the context of imaging?

choices.text: To automate the preauthorization process for elective outpatient imaging studies
To score the appropriateness of imaging orders
To assist radiologists in detecting findings on CT and MRI studies
To generate ICD-10 codes automatically from radiology report text

questions.explanation: CDS software for imaging is technically required for all Medicare outpatient and certain ED patients when ordering advanced imaging tests (CT, MRI, and Nuclear Medicine). The software scores the appropriateness of imaging orders across 8 designated clinical priority conditions using recommendations from Qualified Provider Led Entities (QPLEs), which include national medical societies. The intent is to guide ordering physicians toward the most appropriate studies for their patients. Payment consequences for non-compliance have not yet been defined.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A radiology practice is found to have billed Medicare for imaging studies that were not performed. Under the False Claims Act, which of the following correctly describes the potential financial consequences?

choices.text: Fines of up to the total billed amount per claim filed plus $11,000 per claim filed
Fines of up to two times the billed amount per claim filed plus $11,000 per claim filed
Fines of up to three times the billed amount plus $11,000 per claim filed
A single fine of up to $11,000

questions.explanation: The False Claims Act (FCA) protects the government from being overcharged or sold substandard goods or services. A false claim is generally defined as a request for payment for services that a provider knew or should have known was false or fraudulent. A false claim ruling can result in fines of up to three times the billed amount plus $11,000 per claim filed. Each single exam or service billed to Medicare or Medicaid counts as a separate claim.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: Under HIPAA, which of the following best defines protected health information (PHI)?

choices.text: Any health information stored in an electronic health record system
Individually identifiable health information, regardless of the form in which it is held or transmitted
Health information shared exclusively between a physician and a patient in a clinical encounter
Health information that includes a patient's name and date of birth only

questions.explanation: PHI refers to individually identifiable health information. The HIPAA Privacy Rule establishes national standards for its protection. The HIPAA Security Rule establishes security standards specifically for PHI when held or transferred in electronic form (e-PHI). The Office for Civil Rights (OCR), within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, is responsible for enforcing these rules with civil money penalties.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: Which federal body is responsible for enforcing the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules?

choices.text: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS)
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
The Office for Civil Rights (OCR)
The Joint Commission (TJC)

questions.explanation: The Office for Civil Rights (OCR), within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, has responsibility for enforcing the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules with civil money penalties. The OCR operationalizes the protections in the Privacy Rule by addressing both technical and nontechnical safeguards that organizations must have in place to secure individuals' electronic PHI.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT considered a PHI identifier under HIPAA?

choices.text: A patient's email address
A patient's ZIP code representing a population less than 20,000
A patient's medical record number
A patient's year of birth

questions.explanation: Under HIPAA, "all elements of dates except year" related to an individual - such as birthdate, admission date, discharge date, and date of death - are considered PHI. The year alone is not a PHI identifier. Other examples of identifiers include names, geographic subdivisions smaller than a state (with the noted exception for larger ZIP codes), phone numbers, fax numbers, email addresses, Social Security numbers, and medical record numbers, among 18 total categories.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A radiology report includes the notation: "MRI brain obtained on 03/15." Under HIPAA, which part of this information constitutes a PHI identifier?

choices.text: Neither the modality nor the date constitutes PHI in isolation
The specific date constitutes a PHI identifier
Only the modality (MRI brain) constitutes a PHI identifier
Both the date and modality are PHI only when they appear together in the same record

questions.explanation: Under HIPAA, all elements of dates except the year - including month and day - related to an individual (such as examination date, admission date, or date of birth) are considered PHI identifiers. The year alone is not listed as a PHI identifier. Accordingly, removing or obscuring the specific month and day (while retaining the year) is an important step in de-identification.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: Under HIPAA, an individual's PHI may generally be disclosed without explicit patient authorization in which of the following circumstances?

choices.text: When a hospital administrator requests it for an internal legal proceeding
When required for delivery of care, payment activities, or healthcare operations involving quality or compliance assurance
When a medical student requests it for an educational case presentation
When a family member who is not the healthcare proxy requests information about the patient's diagnosis

questions.explanation: As a general rule, PHI cannot be disclosed or transmitted to anyone other than the individual without that individual's authorization. Exceptions include information disclosed when necessary for: 1) the delivery of care or treatment, 2) payment activities, and 3) healthcare operations involving quality or competency assurance, fraud or abuse detection, or compliance.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A public health authority contacts a hospital requesting PHI for a patient believed to have a reportable communicable disease. Under HIPAA, can this information be disclosed without the patient's authorization?

choices.text: No, HIPAA prohibits disclosure to any third party without patient authorization
Yes, PHI may be disclosed to public health authorities without patient authorization when required by law
Yes, but only if the patient is deceased
Yes, if the patient has previously signed a blanket disclosure authorization

questions.explanation: HIPAA permits PHI to be disclosed without patient authorization when required by law in several circumstances, including: disclosure to public health authorities, during investigation of abuse, neglect, or domestic violence, to oversight agencies, for judicial and administrative proceedings, for law enforcement purposes, and for worker's compensation. Disclosure to public health authorities is one of the most commonly encountered exceptions.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A court issues a subpoena requesting a patient's radiology records as part of a civil lawsuit. Which of the following is accurate under HIPAA?

choices.text: PHI may be disclosed for judicial and administrative proceedings without patient authorization when required by law
PHI cannot be disclosed in any judicial proceeding without explicit patient consent
PHI may only be disclosed in criminal, not civil, judicial proceedings
PHI requires a court order signed by a federal judge before disclosure in any judicial proceeding

questions.explanation: HIPAA includes judicial and administrative proceedings among the circumstances in which PHI may be disclosed without patient authorization when required by law. Additional situations where disclosure without authorization is permitted include public health authorities, law enforcement purposes, oversight agencies, worker's compensation, and investigation of abuse or neglect.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of an Institutional Review Board (IRB)?

choices.text: To review and monitor research involving human subjects
To approve billing practices for research-related imaging studies
To credential radiologists performing research-related procedures
To enforce HIPAA compliance within research institutions

questions.explanation: Under FDA regulations, an IRB has the authority to approve, require modifications to secure approval, or deny approval for proposed research protocols. IRBs serve to protect the rights and welfare of human research subjects. They are required to ensure diversity of membership - including consideration of race, gender, and cultural backgrounds - and must register with the Department of Health and Human Services.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A radiologist proposes a project to analyze imaging turnaround times at her institution in order to improve reporting efficiency for patients with suspected stroke. She asks whether IRB approval is required. Which of the following is most accurate?

choices.text: IRB approval is always required whenever patient imaging data is reviewed
IRB approval is required because the project involves patient imaging data
IRB approval may not be required
IRB approval is not required as long as fewer than 50 patients are included

questions.explanation: IRBs typically provide an exemption from formal protocol review when a project constitutes a quality improvement activity, as long as the primary objective is to improve local practice rather than to create generalizable knowledge. Additionally, IRB approval is not required for studies that do not meet federal definitions of human subjects research, such as studies utilizing open-source public datasets.
