questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A researcher proposes a large retrospective study reviewing archived radiology images with no patient contact and minimal risk. Which of the following is most accurate regarding the need for informed consent?

choices.text: Not required, as the research involves no more than minimal risks to participants and probably could not be carried out without a waiver for consent
Not required, as is always the case for retrospective studies
Informed consent is always required for any research using patient imaging data
Informed consent can only be waived if all patients in the study are deceased

questions.explanation: An IRB may waive the requirement for informed consent when the research involves no more than minimal risks to participants and cannot practically be carried out without such a waiver. Retrospective review of imaging is the classic example - individual patient contact is not feasible, the risk is minimal, and the scientific value can justify proceeding under IRB oversight without individual consent.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: Approximately what percentage of radiologists are named in a medical malpractice lawsuit each year?
questions.explanation: Approximately 7% of all radiologists are named in a medical malpractice lawsuit each year. Radiology indemnity payments in malpractice cases average approximately $480,000, and the average radiologist spends approximately 19 months of his or her career with an unresolved open malpractice claim. More than 90% of physicians report that they at least sometimes engage in defensive medicine.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A radiologist switches jobs and learns that her current malpractice policy requires her to purchase tail insurance upon departure. Which type of policy does she most likely have, and why is tail insurance necessary?

choices.text: A claims-made policy; it only protects the physician while the policy is in effect
An occurrence policy; tail insurance extends coverage to new employers
A claims-made policy; it covers all events regardless of when the claim is filed
An occurrence policy; it does not cover procedure-related complications

questions.explanation: Claims-made policies - the most common type of malpractice insurance - protect physicians from personal financial liability only while the policy is in effect. When a physician changes jobs or retires, tail insurance must be arranged to ensure continued coverage for events that occurred during the active policy period but for which claims may be filed afterward. In contrast, occurrence policies cover any claim for an event that took place during the period of coverage, even if the claim is filed after the policy lapses.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A patient files a malpractice lawsuit against a radiologist for a missed lung nodule. Which of the following is NOT required to be established for the claim to succeed as medical negligence?

choices.text: Breach of duty
Damages
Level of experience
Causation

questions.explanation: Medical malpractice lawsuits are based on the tort of negligence and require four elements: 1) an established duty to the patient, 2) a breach of duty (failure to meet the standard of care), 3) causation (the breach was the proximate cause of the patient's injuries), and 4) damages. All four elements must be demonstrated. Even if a finding was missed, establishing causation can be difficult - for example, attributing a subsequent hemorrhagic stroke to a missed lung nodule would be challenging to support.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following represents the most common cause of malpractice lawsuits against radiologists?

choices.text: Adverse contrast media reactions
Procedural complications
Alleged errors in diagnosis
Communication deficiencies

questions.explanation: The most common cause of malpractice lawsuits against radiologists is for alleged errors in diagnosis. Negligent diagnosis claims generally fall into three categories: 1) failures of perception (not identifying a finding), 2) failures of interpretation (identifying a finding but not appropriately appreciating or adequately communicating its significance), and 3) combinations of both.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A radiologist reviews a chest CT and dictates a detailed report describing bilateral lower lobe consolidations consistent with pneumonia. A 1.2 cm spiculated right upper lobe nodule clearly visible on the images is not mentioned anywhere in the report. A subsequent radiologist identifies the nodule six months later. This error is best classified as which of the following?

choices.text: A failure of perception
A failure of interpretation
A system error related to workflow
A communication deficiency

questions.explanation: This case represents a failure of perception - the radiologist did not identify the finding at all. Failures of perception are cognitive errors of visual scanning, recognition, or interpretation. They are distinct from failures of interpretation, in which a finding is identified but its significance is not appropriately appreciated or communicated. System errors are related to health system issues or context of care delivery rather than individual cognitive performance.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A radiologist reviewing a CT abdomen correctly identifies and describes a 2 cm low-attenuation hepatic lesion in the findings section of the report. The impression reads: "No acute abnormality." The lesion is subsequently found to be hepatocellular carcinoma. This error is best classified as which of the following?

choices.text: A failure of interpretation
A failure of perception
A cognitive error of visual scanning
A system error due to incomplete clinical history

questions.explanation: This represents a failure of interpretation - the radiologist identified the finding but did not appropriately appreciate or adequately communicate its significance. The lesion was perceived but was not carried forward into the impression with appropriate characterization or follow-up recommendation. Failures of interpretation are distinct from failures of perception, in which the finding is not identified at all.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A busy academic radiology department implements a policy requiring radiologists to read a minimum of 80 studies per half-day shift. Shortly thereafter, the department notes an increase in missed findings on chest radiographs. Which of the following best describes the type of error contributing to this pattern?

choices.text: System errors
Cognitive errors
A failure of the informed consent process
Communication deficiencies

questions.explanation: System errors are related to health system issues or context of care delivery. Certain system factors - including lighting conditions, shift length, and pace of interpretation - have been shown to increase the likelihood of diagnostic errors. An institutionally imposed workload that increases pace of interpretation represents a system-level contributor to missed findings, rather than an individual failure of cognitive perception or interpretation.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A radiologist's chest CT interpretation that missed a lung mass is reviewed two years later as part of a malpractice case. Several expert witnesses reviewing the images state they would have clearly identified the lesion and that missing it represented negligence. Their confidence in retrospect is largely driven by knowing the patient's eventual diagnosis. This phenomenon is referred to as which of the following?

choices.text: Hindsight bias
Anchoring bias
Confirmation bias
Satisfaction of search

questions.explanation: Hindsight bias refers to the tendency for people with knowledge of the actual outcome of a case to believe falsely that they would have predicted its outcome. In radiology malpractice, hindsight bias makes defending diagnostic error cases particularly difficult, as retrospective reviewers who know the diagnosis often rate findings as more conspicuous than they were at the time of the original interpretation.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A radiologist performs a CT-guided lung biopsy using an 18-gauge needle via a transfissural trajectory. The patient develops a pneumothorax requiring chest tube placement. A malpractice claim is subsequently filed. Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the claim of negligence?

choices.text: The radiologist used an overly large needle and chose a trajectory that unnecessarily crossed aerated lung
The patient had a history of a prior pneumothorax
The radiologist documented the risk of pneumothorax during the informed consent process
The patient was observed for two hours with a stable post-procedural chest radiograph before discharge

questions.explanation: Complications alone do not indicate negligence. However, malpractice claims based on procedural complications are more successfully argued when the radiologist did not exercise appropriate care in minimizing the risk of the complication, identifying it once it occurred, or treating it. Using an overly large needle or selecting a trajectory that unnecessarily crosses aerated lung speaks directly to a failure to minimize complication risk, making this the strongest basis for a negligence argument.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: Following a CT-guided biopsy, a patient develops an enlarging pneumothorax. No post-procedural chest radiograph is obtained, and the patient is discharged home. She returns to the emergency department the next morning in respiratory distress. The patient's family pursues litigation. Beyond the failures in clinical management, what additional factor does the text identify as making patients and families more likely to sue in such situations?

choices.text: The belief that details of their care were withheld from them
The absence of a signed procedure consent form
The procedure was performed by a trainee rather than an attending radiologist
The referring physician was not notified of the complication

questions.explanation: Patients and their families are more likely to sue for damages related to procedural complications when they believe that details of their care were withheld. Most risk managers therefore advocate for full and prompt disclosure of any untoward events and ongoing communication about decision-making and treatment. Detailed and contemporaneous documentation in the procedure report and medical record may also prove helpful in any subsequent legal proceeding.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the legal status of informed consent for invasive radiologic procedures?

choices.text: Informed consent is a courtesy gesture and carries no independent legal weight in malpractice cases
Informed consent is legally required only for procedures performed under general anesthesia
Informed consent requires a signed form but has no requirement for discussion of specific procedural risks
Informed consent is codified in U.S. courts as a basic right of self-determination

questions.explanation: The doctrine of informed consent has been codified in U.S. courts as a basic right of self-determination. Courts have subsequently expanded this doctrine to apply to procedures other than open operations and those performed by nonsurgeon physicians, including radiologists. Engaging patients (and their families, when appropriate) in decision-making before a procedure also helps set realistic expectations and may be protective in the event of a subsequent negligence claim.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: In radiology, what does "routine communication" refer to?

choices.text: Verbal communication between the radiologist and the ordering physician
Telephone calls made for all imaging findings regardless of urgency
Standardized templates used for communicating critical results
The creation and delivery of written radiology reports

questions.explanation: In radiology, routine communication refers to the creation and delivery of written reports. The final report represents the definitive documentation of the results of an imaging examination or procedure. The ACR Practice Parameter for Communication of Diagnostic Imaging Findings outlines suggested formatting, including patient identifying information, examination details, and report content recommendations such as findings, impressions, limitations, and complications.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A radiologist identifies a new, large pneumothorax on a portable chest radiograph in a post-operative patient on the surgical floor. How should this finding be classified?

choices.text: A Level 1 result
A Level 2 result
A Level 3 result
A Level 4 result

questions.explanation: A large pneumothorax is a classic example of a critical (Level 1) result - a finding that may be considered life threatening and that requires urgent or emergent clinical attention. Communication requires direct contact between the radiologist and the requesting clinician or another licensed healthcare provider responsible for the patient's care, generally expected within 60 minutes of the observation being made, and must be documented. Level 2 results are findings that could result in mortality or significant morbidity if not treated in a timely manner but are less immediately dire than Level 1, generally warranting communication within 12 hours - examples include an intra-abdominal abscess or impending pathological fracture. Level 3 results are findings that are potentially significant but not time-sensitive, where mechanisms must be in place to ensure the finding is not overlooked - examples include a newly identified lung nodule or solid renal mass.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A radiologist identifies an intra-abdominal abscess on an outpatient CT abdomen in a patient with fever. Which of the following best describes the appropriate communication approach?

choices.text: Communication via the final written report alone is sufficient
Direct physician contact is expected within 60 minutes
Mechanisms must ensure the finding is not overlooked, but communication timing is not specifically defined
Communication is generally expected within 12 hours via direct call

questions.explanation: An intra-abdominal abscess is an example of a Level 2 finding - new or unexpected findings that could result in mortality or significant morbidity if not treated in a timely manner, but that are less immediately dire than critical results. These findings generally warrant communication within 12 hours. The radiologist might call the care team directly or request a call service to make contact on his or her behalf.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A radiologist identifies a new 8 mm solid pulmonary nodule in a 62-year-old former smoker on a CT obtained for an unrelated indication. Which of the following best describes the recommended communication approach?

choices.text: Direct telephone contact with the ordering physician within 60 minutes
Direct physician contact within 12 hours
No nonroutine communication is needed; the finding can be addressed solely through the routine final written report
May be reported electronically when tracking confirmation is in place

questions.explanation: A newly identified lung nodule is an example of a Level 3 finding - significant but not immediately time-sensitive. Mechanisms must be in place to ensure these findings are not overlooked. Such findings may be reported electronically when electronic messaging tracking mechanisms are in place to make sure the information was successfully received, supplemented by telephone confirmation when necessary.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following pieces of information should be documented when nonroutine communication of an urgent imaging finding takes place?

choices.text: The patient's insurance information and the cost of the imaging study
A transcript of the conversation between the radiologist and the clinician
The patient's vital signs at the time the communication was made
The date and time of the communication, the person reporting, the person receiving, and a summary of the information conveyed

questions.explanation: Documentation of all nonroutine communication should include: the date and time of the communication, the person reporting the information, the person receiving the information, and a summary of or reference to the information that was conveyed.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A resident is stopped in the hospital corridor by a surgeon who asks for an informal opinion on a CT scan that the surgeon is viewing on his phone - obtained at an outside institution without original reports or comparison studies available. The resident provides an interpretation that the surgeon uses to make a clinical decision. Which of the following best describes the risks and recommended approach?

choices.text: This type of informal consultation carries no additional risk as long as the interpretation is documented in the medical record by the surgeon
Informal consultations of this type are protected from legal discovery when they occur in a recognized clinical care setting
This interaction constitutes formal second-opinion interpretation and should be billed accordingly
This interaction carries additional inherent risk and the radiologist should document it independently from the referring clinician's documentation

questions.explanation: This is an example of a curbside consult - an informal communication that does not result in a formal report but may be used to make treatment decisions. Such interactions often occur in suboptimal viewing conditions and preclude immediate documentation. A key risk is that the referring clinician's documentation may constitute the only written record of the communication. Informal communications are largely discouraged; when they do occur, radiologists should document them independently from the referring clinician's documentation.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A radiologist named in a malpractice lawsuit discussed the case informally with several colleagues in the hallway over the course of several weeks. His attorney advises him that these conversations may be subject to legal discovery. Which of the following best explains why they are not protected?

choices.text: Verbal communications are never protected from discovery in malpractice cases
Attorney-client privilege does not extend to physicians
Protection from discovery applies only to written documentation, not verbal exchanges
The conversations were informal discussions outside established peer review processes

questions.explanation: Most communication related to any part of a malpractice case - whether written or oral - is considered discoverable and can be used as evidence at trial. While most jurisdictions protect certain peer review activities from legal discovery, this protection applies only to communications that occur within established peer review processes. Informal conversations with colleagues outside of such established processes are typically not protected from legal discovery. Physicians involved in lawsuits are strongly discouraged from speaking with any parties other than their attorneys about elements of their cases.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 5: Reimbursement, Regulatory Compliance, and Legal Considerations in Radiology
questions.stem: A radiology department conducts a formal peer review conference to evaluate a case in which a significant finding was missed. A radiologist who participated is later asked to testify in a malpractice proceeding about the recommendations made at the conference. Which of the following best describes whether this testimony can be compelled?

choices.text: All peer review discussions are fully discoverable and may be used in malpractice proceedings
Peer review activities are protected only if the conclusions reached were favorable to the defendant radiologist
Peer review is protected only in federal courts, not in state malpractice proceedings
Participants in an approved peer review process are not required to testify about the findings, recommendations, or evaluations of that process

questions.explanation: Most jurisdictions protect certain peer review activities from legal discovery. Peer review protection laws are designed to provide an incentive for healthcare providers to perform ongoing quality improvement activities without fear of increased tort risk. As a general rule, no person who participates in any approved peer review process shall be permitted or required to testify in any civil action about the findings, recommendations, evaluations, opinions, or other actions of that process. This protection applies only to communications within established peer review processes - informal conversations with colleagues outside those processes are not protected.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: What does the acronym DICOM stand for?

choices.text: Dynamic Imaging and Communications in Medicine
Digital Information Communication in Medicine
Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine
Diagnostic Imaging Computer Output Model

questions.explanation: DICOM stands for Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine. It is the international standard that specifies protocols for the display, transfer, storage, and processing of medical images, and applies to both pixel-based image data and the metadata stored in the DICOM header.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: What does the DICOM standard govern?

choices.text: Exchange of non-image clinical data between healthcare systems
Coding and billing of radiology procedures
Display, transfer, storage, and processing of medical images
Encryption and security of electronic health records

questions.explanation: The DICOM standard governs the display, transfer, storage, and processing of medical images. It applies to both pixel-based image data and metadata. DICOM transactions enable data to be queried, retrieved, and transmitted between systems, and allow order information to be communicated between the RIS and the imaging modality without manual data entry by the technologist.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: In a DICOM imaging study, what information is contained in the DICOM header?

choices.text: The pixel-based image data captured by the imaging modality
Metadata containing information about the image, series, examination, patient, imaging facility, and scanner
The compressed archive file containing the full imaging study
The HL7 transaction used to communicate the imaging order to the modality

questions.explanation: The DICOM header contains the metadata associated with a DICOM image, including information about the image, the series, the examination, the patient, the imaging facility, and the scanner. The data are organized into separate fields, each with a unique identifier, so that specific elements can be queried directly. DICOM transactions enable this data to be queried, retrieved, and transmitted between systems in an organized fashion.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: What is the key distinction between DICOM and HL7 in the context of medical imaging?

choices.text: DICOM is used for administrative data; HL7 is used exclusively for imaging data
DICOM governs the storage and communication of medical images and image-related data; HL7 governs the exchange of non-image medical information
DICOM and HL7 serve identical functions and are used interchangeably in modern radiology systems
DICOM is an international standard; HL7 applies only within the United States

questions.explanation: DICOM governs the display, transfer, storage, and processing of medical images and their associated metadata. HL7 (Health Level 7) is a separate international standards organization responsible for developing standards for the exchange, integration, sharing, and retrieval of non-image medical information. In a typical radiology workflow, both standards are used: HL7 transactions communicate orders between the EMR and RIS, while DICOM transactions communicate imaging data between modalities, PACS, and related systems.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the HL7 V2 messaging standard?

choices.text: A human-readable XML-based standard considered the most widely adopted HL7 standard today
A text-based standard generally considered the most widely implemented healthcare-related standard in the world
A standard designed exclusively for imaging data exchange between PACS and modalities
An internet-based standard that allows software developers to exchange medical data using web transactions

questions.explanation: HL7 V2 is a text-based standard and is generally considered the most widely implemented healthcare-related standard in the world. It facilitates the exchange of medical data by enabling interoperability between many types of electronic medical systems. HL7 V3 is more human-readable but has been less widely adopted due to its increased complexity. HL7 FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is a newer standard that uses internet transactions to exchange medical data between systems.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes HL7 FHIR?

choices.text: The oldest and most widely implemented HL7 standard due to its simplicity
A standard that allows software developers to use internet transactions to exchange medical data between systems
An XML-based standard that is less widely adopted than HL7 V2 due to increased complexity
A standard designed specifically to replace DICOM for imaging data exchange

questions.explanation: HL7 FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is a newer standard that allows software developers to use internet transactions to exchange medical data between systems, increasing the potential for data exchange. HL7 V3, while more human-readable than V2, has been less widely adopted due to its increased complexity. V2 remains the most widely implemented HL7 standard in healthcare today.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the primary function of a Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS)?

choices.text: A software application managing all aspects of an imaging exam, including scheduling, reporting, and billing
The radiologist's primary tool for imaging viewing and interpretation
A central archive supporting storage of both DICOM and non-DICOM data across multiple clinical service lines
An international standard governing the storage and transfer of medical images

questions.explanation: PACS (Picture Archiving and Communication System) is the radiologist's primary tool for imaging viewing and interpretation. Basic components include a workstation, display, short-term storage, and long-term archive. PACS communicates with imaging modalities using DICOM transactions and with the RIS and/or EMR using HL7 transactions. Modern PACS systems can be entirely web-based and accessible on mobile devices as well as desktop thin clients.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: A hospital wants to consolidate storage of imaging data from radiology, cardiology, and the operating room - including both DICOM images and non-DICOM data such as photographs and pathology slides - into a single central repository. Which system is most specifically designed to support this need?

choices.text: PACS (Picture Archiving and Communication System)
RIS (Radiology Information System)
VNA (Vendor-Neutral Archive)
EMR (Electronic Medical Record)

questions.explanation: The vendor-neutral archive (VNA) allows data to be stored in a central archive that supports multiple types of DICOM images across clinical service lines (radiology, cardiology, operating room, etc.) as well as non-DICOM data including photographs and pathology slides. Enterprise imaging relies heavily on VNA technology for this purpose. A key challenge in enterprise imaging is formatting and exchanging the metadata that accompanies non-DICOM images.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the primary function of the Radiology Information System (RIS)?

choices.text: Long-term archival and retrieval of imaging studies for viewing on diagnostic workstations
A software application managing all aspects of an imaging exam
The primary tool used by radiologists for image viewing and interpretation
A standard for transmitting images between radiology departments and referring clinicians

questions.explanation: The radiology information system (RIS) is a software application that manages all aspects of an imaging exam, including order reconciliation, patient scheduling and tracking, communication with modalities and PACS, reporting, results notification, and billing. The RIS may be a standalone application or a component of the EMR. Both PACS and RIS can be used to drive clinical workflow.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: Lossless image compression achieves approximately what compression ratio?
questions.explanation: Lossless compression achieves file size reduction by decreasing redundant image information - for example, the black background of a CT image. Because image content is fully preserved, lossless compression can only reduce image file size by approximately 3:1. Lossy compression allows for more substantial image size reduction (on the order of 10:1) by irreversibly discarding unnecessary or minimally important image information without significantly compromising diagnostic quality.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: A radiologist develops pain and paresthesias in the thumb and index finger of his dominant hand after years of extended mouse use. Physical examination reveals a positive Tinel sign at the wrist. Which repetitive strain injury best explains this presentation?

choices.text: Cubital tunnel syndrome
DeQuervain tenosynovitis
Carpal tunnel syndrome
Lateral epicondylitis

questions.explanation: Carpal tunnel syndrome involves the median nerve and often occurs due to dorsiflexion of the wrist from upward angulation while typing or using a mouse. Symptoms include pain, numbness, and paresthesias in the median nerve distribution. Cubital tunnel syndrome involves the ulnar nerve and can occur at the wrist or elbow. DeQuervain tenosynovitis is an RSI of the thumb. All three are recognized occupational hazards for radiologists.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: Which of the following workstation configurations is recommended to reduce the risk of repetitive strain injury in radiologists?

choices.text: Slight wrist dorsiflexion to reduce fatigue during extended mouse use
Forearm, wrist, and hand maintained parallel to the floor
Monitor positioned below eye level with the wrist elevated above the forearm
Mouse positioned far from the body to encourage shoulder rotation

questions.explanation: Workstation configurations that promote a neutral body position - with the forearm, wrist, and hand parallel to the floor, lumbar support, and appropriate distance between the user and the display - can help decrease the incidence of repetitive strain injuries (RSI) among radiologists. Common RSIs include carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve), cubital tunnel syndrome (ulnar nerve), and DeQuervain tenosynovitis (thumb).

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the sequence of system communications in the standard medical imaging workflow, from order placement to final report delivery?

choices.text: EMR → RIS → DICOM Modality Work List to modality → PACS → RIS and EMR
EMR → DICOM Modality Work List to modality → RIS → PACS → RIS and EMR
EMR → RIS → PACS → DICOM Modality Work List to modality → RIS and EMR
EMR → RIS → DICOM Modality Work List to modality → RIS and EMR → PACS

questions.explanation: The correct sequence begins with an order placed in the EMR, which communicates to the RIS via an HL7 transaction. The RIS then communicates order information to the imaging modality via the DICOM Modality Work List. After image acquisition, the modality communicates images to PACS via DICOM transactions. The radiologist views images on PACS, dictates the report via voice recognition, and the reporting software delivers the final report to the RIS and EMR via HL7 transactions.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a disaster recovery (DR) policy?

choices.text: Systematic precautions and failover routines for routine system failures such as power outages
Procedures governing data encryption and off-site backup locations
Directives for activities to be followed in the event of a large-scale, unexpected, highly disruptive event
Federal compliance requirements for electronic health record security

questions.explanation: Disaster recovery (DR) policies direct activities that should be followed in the event of a disaster - a large-scale, unexpected, highly disruptive event, whether natural or human in origin. DR policies typically include a description of off-site data backup systems, the frequency of backup cycles, and the steps required to restore critical data in the event of a disruption.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a business continuity (BC) policy?

choices.text: Steps to restore critical data following a large-scale catastrophic event
Systematic precautions, backups, and failover routines to maintain patient care during routine system failures
Off-site data backup procedures required by federal regulation
Directives for responding to a natural disaster or ransomware attack

questions.explanation: Business continuity (BC) policies refer to the systematic precautions, backups, and failover routines required to continue caring for patients when a system failure occurs under otherwise routine working conditions - such as a power outage. BC policies are distinct from disaster recovery policies, which address large-scale, highly disruptive events rather than everyday operational failures.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: What is the expected uptime of a high-availability system?

choices.text: 99.9% uptime
99.99% uptime
99.999% uptime
100% uptime

questions.explanation: Radiology systems are considered high-availability (HA) systems, which must have the ability to perform automated recovery and failover operations in the event of service disruption. The uptime expectations of an HA system are expressed as a "number of nines." PACS is generally expected to perform at "four nines" - 99.99% uptime - which translates to no more than approximately 50 minutes of downtime per year.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes fault tolerance (FT) in the context of radiology information systems?

choices.text: The ability of a system to continue functioning if one of its components fails
The maximum acceptable time for a system to recover after a total failure
The percentage of time a system operates without any service interruption
The process of backing up data to an off-site location to prevent data loss

questions.explanation: Fault tolerance (FT) refers to the ability of a system to continue functioning if one of its components fails. To avoid single points of failure, redundancy is built into essential components of radiology systems - including servers, network connections, and data archives. This built-in redundancy is what allows high-availability systems to achieve the high uptime expectations required in a clinical environment.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: A radiology department experiences a ransomware attack that encrypts all imaging files and systems. Which of the following best describes why standard downtime procedures may be insufficient in this scenario?

choices.text: Standard downtime procedures are designed primarily for brief, localized failures
Ransomware attacks only affect PACS and do not compromise the RIS or EMR
Federal law prohibits radiology departments from operating under analog workflows
Ransomware events are covered by business continuity policies that guarantee full system recovery within 24 hours

questions.explanation: Ransomware attacks occur when bad actors encrypt files and systems and demand a ransom for the decryption key. Unlike routine downtime events, a ransomware attack may require an extended recovery period during which typical downtime procedures may be insufficient. A long-term analog workflow - such as a paper-based system - may be necessary to maintain business continuity while compromised systems are isolated and data recovery is attempted. Any recovered data will eventually need to be reconciled with new data collected after the attack.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: What is the key distinction between de-identification and anonymization of medical imaging data?

choices.text: De-identification may still allow re-identification using a key; anonymization removes all PHI such that identity cannot be re-established
De-identification removes all PHI permanently; anonymization allows re-identification using a key
De-identification applies only to image pixel data; anonymization applies only to metadata
De-identification and anonymization are interchangeable terms referring to the same process

questions.explanation: De-identification involves removing PHI from an imaging examination such that patient identity cannot be directly determined from the images or metadata. However, de-identified images may still contain information that enables an approved entity to re-identify the patient using a key. Anonymization goes further - it removes all PHI and other identifiable data such that the patient's identity cannot be re-established in the future.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: A researcher is planning to de-identify a dataset of head CT scans for a multicenter research study. A colleague warns that the imaging data may still be considered PHI even after removal of all DICOM header metadata. Why?

choices.text: The contours of a patient's face can be reconstructed from CT or MRI of the head, making imaging that includes the face PHI
All CT head images are automatically considered PHI regardless of the de-identification method used
CT head imaging always contains burned-in patient identifiers that cannot be removed with standard tools
Metadata removal alone is insufficient; only full anonymization meets HIPAA requirements for research

questions.explanation: Because the contours of a patient's face can be reconstructed from CT or MRI of the head, imaging that includes the face is considered PHI. This means that in addition to removing DICOM header metadata, facial surface data must also be addressed as part of a complete de-identification process for head imaging datasets.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: A researcher is attempting to de-identify a dataset of ultrasound images for a research study. A data specialist notes that standard automated de-identification tools may be insufficient. What is the most likely reason?

choices.text: Ultrasound images often contain burned-in PHI within the image pixel data itself that must be separately removed
Ultrasound images use a proprietary DICOM format incompatible with standard de-identification tools
Ultrasound studies are not subject to HIPAA de-identification requirements
Automated de-identification tools are validated only for CT and MRI datasets

questions.explanation: In some imaging modalities such as ultrasound, PHI may be "burned in" to the image pixel data itself - appearing as visible text overlaid on the image rather than existing only in the DICOM header metadata. Standard automated de-identification processes that strip header metadata may not remove this burned-in PHI, which must be separately addressed to fully de-identify the images.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: A neuroradiology researcher wants to quantify the volumes of gray matter and white matter in patients with Alzheimer's disease to study cortical atrophy patterns. Which image post-processing technique would be the essential first step in this analysis?

choices.text: Image registration
Maximum intensity projection (MIP)
Segmentation
Curved planar reformation (CPR)

questions.explanation: Segmentation involves isolating or extracting a region of interest from an image or extracting a subset of images from an image stack for further analysis. Segmentation of gray matter and white matter from brain MRI may be the first step toward more advanced analysis of atrophy in neurodegenerative disorders. This is distinct from image registration, which involves aligning two image sets to allow direct spatial comparison.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: A radiologist is comparing pre- and post-treatment MRI studies of a patient with a brain tumor. The imaging software aligns the two scans so that corresponding anatomic structures occupy the same spatial coordinates, enabling direct comparison of lesion size. Which post-processing technique does this represent?

choices.text: Image registration
Segmentation
Maximum intensity projection (MIP)
Volume rendering

questions.explanation: Image registration involves aligning one image set onto the coordinate space of another to allow more direct comparison of the two image sets. Deformations used in registration can be rigid (translation, scaling), affine (shearing), or elastic. Elastic deformation involves local warping of an image to better align it with the reference image and can accommodate changes such as patient position, lung expansion, or soft tissue shape changes.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: A radiologist reviewing a CT pulmonary angiogram asks the technologist to generate images that display the highest-attenuation voxels along rays projected through a slab of tissue, optimizing visualization of contrast-filled pulmonary arteries. Which post-processing technique is being requested?

choices.text: Multiplanar reformation (MPR)
Curved planar reformation (CPR)
Maximum intensity projection (MIP)
Volume rendering

questions.explanation: Maximum intensity projection (MIP) selects and displays the highest-attenuation voxels along rays projected through a volume or slab of tissue, making it well suited for visualizing contrast-filled vessels. MIPs are a form of simple 3-D post-processing that can be performed on most modern PACS. More elaborate techniques - such as curved planar reformats (CPRs), functional analysis, and cinematic rendering - may require additional thin-client software and a dedicated 3-D lab.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: A vascular surgeon requests a post-processing technique that will allow her to visualize the entire course of a tortuous renal artery in a single 2-D image by "unfolding" the vessel along its centerline. Which technique is most appropriate?

choices.text: Maximum intensity projection (MIP)
Volume rendering
Curved planar reformation (CPR)
Segmentation

questions.explanation: A curved planar reformation (CPR) straightens a tortuous vessel along its centerline, allowing the entire lumen to be visualized in a single reformatted image. CPRs are considered more elaborate post-processing and may require additional thin-client software beyond what is available on a standard PACS workstation, potentially supported by a dedicated 3-D lab team. Simple 3-D post-processing such as MPRs, MIPs, and volume rendering can generally be performed on most modern PACS.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly distinguishes artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL)?

choices.text: AI is the broadest field; ML is a subfield of AI; DL is a subfield of ML
AI, ML, and DL are interchangeable terms for the same technology
ML is the broadest field; AI is a subfield of ML; DL is a subfield of AI
DL is the broadest field; ML and AI are subfields applied specifically to image and text analysis

questions.explanation: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the field of computer science that gives computers the ability to mimic human intelligence. Machine learning (ML) is a subfield of AI that enables computers to learn a task without an explicit set of instructions. Deep learning (DL) is a further subfield that uses multi-layered neural networks with weighted connections to analyze data and works with both images and text. AI currently serves as an adjunct to the human radiologist; few fully autonomous AI applications exist for radiology.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: A research team trains an AI algorithm by exposing it to 50,000 chest radiographs, each labeled by expert radiologists as either "normal" or "abnormal." The model is then evaluated on a separate set of 10,000 labeled images it has never previously seen. What type of machine learning is being used?

choices.text: Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Supervised learning
Transfer learning

questions.explanation: This describes supervised learning, in which an algorithm is exposed to a labeled set of training data and then evaluated on how well it predicts labels on a separate, non-overlapping test set. The use of pre-defined labels (normal/abnormal) provided by expert annotators is the defining feature of supervised learning. It is critical that the test set not overlap with the training data, so that model performance is not artificially exaggerated.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: A research team feeds an AI algorithm thousands of radiology reports without providing any labels or predefined categories. Without further guidance, the algorithm independently identifies clusters of reports with similar language patterns. What type of machine learning is being used?

choices.text: Supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Transfer learning
Unsupervised learning

questions.explanation: This describes unsupervised learning, in which an algorithm is exposed to data without pre-defined labels or categories and is expected to organize the data on its own. Unlike supervised learning, there is no labeled training set for the model to learn from. Unsupervised models must be validated and may not perform as well as supervised models without further training.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: An AI model trained to detect pulmonary nodules on chest CTs from a large academic medical center is deployed at a community hospital and performs significantly worse than its internal validation metrics predicted. Which of the following best explains this discrepancy?

choices.text: The model was overfitted to the training data
Automation bias caused clinicians to over-rely on the model at the community hospital
Data drift occurred because the training data was collected before the model was deployed
The test set overlapped with the training data

questions.explanation: Overfitting occurs when a model is trained so closely to a specific dataset that it performs very well on similar data from the same organization but does not perform as well on data that differ in some way - such as data from another institution. This is a common pitfall in AI model training and underscores the importance of external validation before deployment.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: Why is it critical that the test set used to evaluate an AI model does not overlap with its training data?

choices.text: Overlapping data increases the computational processing time required for model training
Overlapping data causes the model to become overfitted to the test set rather than the training set
Overlapping data violates HIPAA because the same patient data is used for two different purposes
Overlapping data artificially exaggerates model performance

questions.explanation: In supervised machine learning, it is important that test set data not overlap with training data so that model performance is not artificially exaggerated. If the model has already been exposed to the test data during training, its performance metrics will not accurately reflect how well it will perform on new, unseen data in the real-world clinical environment.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: Before being input into a deep learning model for image analysis, radiology images typically undergo pre-processing that may include downsampling by as much as 10x. What is a potential consequence of this downsampling?

choices.text: The model becomes more prone to overfitting on the training data
The model's output layer cannot accept inputs below a minimum resolution threshold
Downsampling increases the risk of data drift after model deployment
The decrease in image resolution may reduce the conspicuity of subtle findings

questions.explanation: Image data for deep learning models are pre-processed before use, which may include rescaling, cropping, denoising, histogram equalization, and often downsampling - sometimes by as much as 10x. This decrease in image resolution may reduce the conspicuity of subtle findings in images unless a sufficient number of training examples containing those findings are provided during model development.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes a common application of natural language processing (NLP) in radiology?

choices.text: Automated generation of diagnostic images from structured clinical data
Segmentation of anatomic structures from volumetric imaging datasets
Real-time translation of voice dictation into structured DICOM metadata
Detection of critical findings or follow-up recommendations within radiology reports

questions.explanation: Natural language processing (NLP) is the analysis of human language data. Common applications of NLP in radiology include: detection of critical findings or follow-up recommendations, longitudinal lesion monitoring, assessment of report compliance with practice requirements, and radiology-pathology correlation. Text data are pre-processed before NLP model input - including removal of stop words and punctuation, conversion to lowercase, and tokenization - sometimes converting words and phrases to numeric representations through a process called embedding.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: A radiology AI company deploys a model to detect intracranial hemorrhage on non-contrast head CTs. Over the following 18 months, the model's sensitivity gradually declines without any changes to the model itself. Which deployment challenge best explains this phenomenon?

choices.text: Automation bias among the radiologists using the model
Overfitting to the original test dataset
Sampling bias in the original training data
Data drift

questions.explanation: Data drift refers to the degradation of model performance over time due to gradual changes in the data the model processes. This can occur when patient populations, imaging protocols, scanner hardware, or clinical workflows change after model deployment. Models should be monitored after deployment to identify data drift so that retraining or recalibration can be performed when necessary.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: A radiologist consistently accepts AI-generated findings without applying independent clinical judgment, even when the AI output conflicts with her own impression. This behavior is best described as which of the following?

choices.text: Data drift
Overfitting
Sampling bias
Automation bias

questions.explanation: Automation bias refers to the tendency of users to assume the computer is more correct than the human practitioner. In radiology, this can manifest as over-reliance on AI outputs without independent critical evaluation. The way radiologists interact with AI should be monitored to guard against automation bias, which can allow AI errors to pass unchallenged rather than being caught by the human reviewer.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: A major challenge in deploying AI in radiology is described as the "black box" problem. Which of the following best characterizes this challenge?

choices.text: The model's training data is proprietary and cannot be reviewed by the deploying institution
The model's output is encoded in a format incompatible with existing PACS systems
The model cannot be updated after deployment without full retraining from scratch
It is difficult to understand how the model produces its results, making it hard to verify when and why errors occur

questions.explanation: A major challenge in deploying AI for radiology is understanding how the "black box" model produces its results. Deep learning models produce outputs through millions of weighted connections without providing an easily interpretable explanation of the reasoning behind those outputs. This makes it difficult to understand when and why errors occur, to ensure reliable performance across all clinical settings, and to build appropriate clinician trust in the model.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes statistical bias in an AI model, and what is sampling bias specifically?

choices.text: Statistical bias is the tendency of users to over-rely on the model; sampling bias is a subtype that occurs in specific clinical settings
Statistical bias refers to degradation of model performance over time; sampling bias is caused by changes in imaging protocol
Statistical bias and sampling bias are interchangeable terms referring to the same phenomenon

Statistical bias results when a model does not represent the true features of the population; sampling bias is a specific form in which training data do not represent the patients to whom the model will ultimately be applied

questions.explanation: Statistical bias results when a model does not represent the true features of the population it is meant to serve. Sampling bias is a specific form of statistical bias in which the data used to train the model do not represent the patients to whom the model will ultimately be applied - for example, a model trained predominantly on imaging from one institution or demographic group may not perform accurately when applied to a different population.

questions.chapterName: Chapter 6: Core Concepts of Imaging Informatics
questions.stem: An AI model trained to predict patient readmission rates assigns lower risk scores to patients from underserved communities, despite similar disease severity to patients from more affluent areas. Investigation reveals that these patients had fewer documented follow-up visits - not because they were healthier, but because they had less access to care. This is an example of which type of AI bias?

choices.text: Sampling bias
Automation bias
Data drift
Social bias

questions.explanation: Social bias in AI has the potential to exacerbate health disparities by adversely affecting underrepresented populations. In this example, the model predicted better health outcomes in a population that used healthcare resources less frequently, but failed to account for the fact that reduced utilization was related to access to care rather than actual health status. Social bias can lead to systematically worse model performance for already-disadvantaged patient groups, potentially widening existing health disparities.
